subsubtopic: WARREN HART-ACTION TAKEN VIS-A-VIS TAPE RECORDING-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity pursuant to the provisions of Standing Order 43. On February 27 last, the Solicitor General (Mr. Blais) told Michael Duffy, of the CBC, in an interview regarding the taping of the then solicitor general by Warren Hart:
The recording was made known to the handler after it was done and collective action was taken immediately at that time.
In response to Mr. Duffy's next question as to whether the handler received the tape, the Solicitor General said:
The tape was received and destroyed.

That the Solicitor General, on motions, in connection with the affair of Warren Hart, state the name of the handler to whom he referred, identify the collective action mentioned, reveal who authorized the destruction of the tape, when this was done, by whom, and where.

NOVA SCOTIA-GOVERNMENT URGED TO INITIATE COAL MINING OPERATIONS-MOTION UNDER S O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. In view of the announcement made by the Cape Breton Development Corporation last week on the matter of changing operations at the Prince Mine which will mean, among other things, that some 1,000 applicants for jobs in the coal mines now
listed with Devco from the New Waterford area will be affected, in view of the fact that there are still 1,600 applicants from the Glace Bay area, since the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Gillespie), in a recent meeting with the premiers, urged as part of the national energy policy that a new coal mine in the Donkin area of Cape Breton be started as soon as possible, and in view of the offshore coal drilling program which was begun but not completed last year in Cape Breton, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow):
That this government commence the construction part of the new Donkin mine by April of this year and, also, finish the offshore drilling program during the summer months in order to lay the basis for a secure coal operation in that area of Nova Scotia for at least another generation.

subsubtopic: GRAIN TERMINAL AT YORKTON, SASK.-EXPANSION OF PORT OF CHURCHILL-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:

The commissioned report of a consulting firm headed by Mr. Rod Bryden, to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang), rejected an inland grain terminal for Yorkton, Saskatchewan and dismissed, as a consequence, any expansion of the port of Churchill. speakeroldname: Mr. Joe Clark (Leader of the Opposition):
subsubtopic: REQUESTED REDUCTION IN PUBLIC SERVICE HIRING AND GOVERNMENT SPENDING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Finance: It relates to the most recent report of lay-offs reported by Canada employment centres. I should point out that they are reporting lay-offs only of 50 or more persons. They indicate that in the month of February this year, almost 13,000 Canadians were laid off, the great bulk of those in the province of Ontario which is supposed to be one of the healthy provinces in this confederation.
Given the fact that the Chrysler plant, which suffered some 6,800 of these lay-offs in Windsor, has reported that car sales in the first two months of this year are down 22 per cent, and given the large scale of lay-offs generally, I wonder if the Minister of Finance will not accept that these figures are an indication that the mild stimulus he presented in his minibudget statement last fall has not worked and that there is need for more permanent stimulus. Will he now reconsider accepting the proposal of this party to bring in permanent tax cuts paid for by a freeze in public service hiring and other cuts in government spending?

subtopic: CALL FOR BUDGET TO IMPROVE SITUATION

speakeroldname: Mr. Joe Clark (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: CALL FOR BUDGET TO IMPROVE SITUATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, once again the Minister of Finance refuses to address himself to his responsibility of trying to generate jobs and growth in this economy. In the face of these new statistics which indicate at least another 13,000 Canadians out of work last year because of the policies of this government, it is very clear that it is far too late to simply sit back and do nothing.
Will the minister reconsider, and give us a clear commitment, now, that he will bring in a new budget quickly? If he will not accept my proposal, he should at least try to understand it instead of misrepresent it. Will the minister at least consider reducing the federal manufacturing sales tax as a means of specific stimulus to the Canadian manufacturing sector, where most of the lay-offs are occurring?

subtopic: CALL FOR BUDGET TO IMPROVE SITUATION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in terms of the reduction of sales tax, I discussed that proposition with the provinces in the fall. I urged the provinces to again look into that matter when we had our meeting in January. The provinces did not accept a cut in sales tax. One problem with cutting the federal sales tax is that we cannot be sure that the reduction in cost would be passed on to the consumer. That is why we decided on another type of incentive when we introduced our tax incentives last October 20. We have cut taxes in the Canadian economy to the tune of $2 billion since January 1, 1978.

subtopic: CALL FOR BUDGET TO IMPROVE SITUATION
speechtext: The October tax incentive is gone: it obviously has not worked. The new figures indicate that, on the narrow reporting base, another 13,000 Canadians are out of work because of this government. If the minister will not act on a tax cut and reduce the federal sales tax, what does he propose to do to stop this continuing decline in the Canadian economy and give jobs to Canadians who have a right to expect jobs in an economy like ours?

subtopic: CALL FOR BUDGET TO IMPROVE SITUATION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the best thing we can do is to ensure that Canadian products are more competitive than before. It is evident that the policies we are following are working toward that end. We have increased our trade surplus in foreign trade by more than $2 billion, and the competitive position in Canada is improving every month. That is the way to bring back stability and prosperity in this land.

subtopic: CALL FOR BUDGET TO IMPROVE SITUATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance continues to try to play hocus-pocus with the real figures of the Canadian economy. I ask the Minister of Finance, or any other minister competent to answer, why Canadian Manpower statistics which normally, up until this month, were reporting lay-offs of 20 or more, are now reporting only lay-offs of 50 or more, so that the aggregate figures will look smaller and the
Oral Questions
impact of creating unemployment by this government will look less.
Why has there been a change in the reporting base of the Canada employment centres across the country? Is it simply to hide from Canadians the reality of the harm being done to the Canadian economy by this government?

subtopic: CALL FOR BUDGET TO IMPROVE SITUATION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I do not understand what the Leader of the Opposition is suggesting. Is he now accusing Statistics Canada of not issuing statistics that are relevant to Canada whereas a few days ago, when I was not in total agreement with the statistics, he was urging me to accept them even before the possible revision? I for one am not sure if he is accusing Statistics Canada, but I think he would be very ill advised to do so. At any rate, I will ask the Minister of Employment and Immigration to give further explanations to the Leader of the Opposition if possible.

subtopic: REASON ONTARIO HAS SUFFERED HEAVY LAY-OFFS
REASON ONTARIO HAS SUFFERED HEAVY LAY-OFFS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is to the Minister of Finance. Faced with the worst lay-off report ever published by Canada Manpower-this was referred to by my leader-and bearing in mind that 87 per cent of the lay-offs reported in February were in the province of Ontario, would the minister indicate, First, whether he was aware of the impact on Ontario of these lay-offs and, second, can he suggest to the House and the people of Canada any reason why Ontario, in particular, should have suffered such heavy lay-offs?

subtopic: REASON ONTARIO HAS SUFFERED HEAVY LAY-OFFS
speechtext: I have discussed the economic problems of Ontario many times with the Treasurer of Ontario. He will be disclosing his budget tomorrow, I believe, in his own House. We have tried to co-ordinate our economic policies, and following suggestions they have made to me, I have made a proposition to help the provinces to cut the sales tax in order to stimulate demand. But the other provinces have never accepted that proposition. Tomorrow we shall see what Mr. McKeough intends to propose specifically for Ontario. As far as present economic policies are concerned, we debated them with the ministers concerned and at the first ministers' conference and there was no pressure upon us to change them.

Speaking about coordination, the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce, in his "Report from Parliament Hill" appearing in the Hanna Herald on February 15 of this year, stated:
It now seems that the European Community, the United States and Canada will strive for a 40 per cent cut in tariffs.

March 6, 1978
Oral Questions
Would the minister indicate, in the context of the February lay-offs, if it is Canadian policy to cut tariffs by 40 per cent?

We are presently engaged at Geneva in tariff negotiations with other nations to make sure that international trade increases rather than diminishes. At this moment we have not decided what the final position of the government will be. I think it is very important that all the nations of the world make sure that there is a better climate for trading in the world, across the board, so that everyone will benefit, as opposed to going to extreme protectionist policies. What we should like to know is whether the opposition parties have any position between the free trade sympathies of the west and the protectionism of Ontario.

subtopic: IMPACT OF FOOD PRICES ON CPI
IMPACT OF FOOD PRICES ON CPI
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Finance. A few days ago, the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce stated that the impact of food prices on the calculation of the consumer price index will be revised starting in early summer. He further stated that the food component, which presently accounts for about 28 per cent of the consumer price index, is likely to drop to 20 per cent. Will the hon. gentleman tell the House why the government has decided to mislead the public-I can only think of it in those terms-into believing a reduction in the cost of living will take place in the early summer by manipulating the consumer price index statistics in this obvious fashion?

subtopic: IMPACT OF FOOD PRICES ON CPI
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I do not think the government's policy consists in giving orders to Statistics Canada. That organization of the Canadian government has been working in a scientific and very professional way for many years. Nobody but the organization itself decides which base is best for the establishment of statistics relating to Canada's economic performance and traditionally, the government has never intervened in these matters. When I was Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce, I defended on many occasions in the House the integrity, the sincerity and the competence of Statistics Canada and if the organization is now bringing changes in this field, a matter I am not aware of, I am sure that it proceeds this way for reasons of a purely scientific nature.

subtopic: IMPACT OF FOOD PRICES ON CPI
speechtext:
A number of countries, including the United States, use a variety of indexes to measure the cost of living. Will the minister not agree that the announced intention to change the statistical basis and reduce the weight of the food component, which has increased by more than 15 per cent in the last year, will likely have the effect of showing at least a decline in the rate of increase of the index, and that this change, particularly for pensioners and other low income people, could distort reality because these people spend a much

higher proportion of their income on food than do upper income Canadians?

subtopic: IMPACT OF FOOD PRICES ON CPI
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I explained earlier that it is up to Statistics Canada to make those judgments in terms of their conscience and of trying to find out exactly what are the components in increases in the price of food in Canada. It could be that they have decided, because of realities, that Canadians are spending less of their income on food; I do not know, and I do not want to pass judgment. I would rather let Statistics Canada-an institution with a great reputation for making professional and scientific decisions-make that judgment, rather than myself pass judgment on the quality of work Statistics Canada is doing not for the government but for Canada.

subtopic: IMPACT OF FOOD PRICES ON CPI
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the minister knows very well that there have been studies on the possibility, for example, of a separate index for pensioners, as well as for other groups. The minister knows that the government can make a recommendation to Statistics Canada to publish a comparable, different set of figures showing what is really happening in the economy. Does the minister think that changing the procedures which are likely going to show a decline in the cost of living precisely at the time of the next election is a mere coincidence?

subtopic: IMPACT OF FOOD PRICES ON CPI
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I know of no instruction from the government on that matter. It is up to Statistics Canada to prepare the statistics the way they think is the fairest way for the people of Canada to be informed. We do not give instructions to Statistics Canada. I do not know of any such instruction. If Statistics Canada is changing its procedures, I suppose it is because they have a good, professional reason for doing so.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Transport: it relates to a rather disturbing report of a study presented to him by a firm of consultants headed by Mr. Rod Bryden. This study was commissioned in response to a Hall commission recommenda-

March 6, 1978
Oral Questions
tion concerning the construction of an inland terminal at Yorkton, Saskatchewan, to augment shipment of precleaned grain to the port of Churchill. speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subsubtopic: INLAND TERMINAL AT YORKTON, SASK-GOVERNMENT INTENTIONS REGARDING CONSTRUCTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Saskatoon-Biggar is completely wrong in his statement as to the conclusions of the report. It was a report into the question of the cost of developing either a single terminal elevator in the Yorkton area, or several in that region. It analyses those costs and indicates very significant costs indeed. That may be done either way, particularly if a large terminal is used as a feeder for the Churchill terminal which is available for only a very short season; therefore, the gathering of grain has to be concentrated in a short period.
That is what the report covered; it did not include the entire question, by any means. It was a necessary consultants' study about the complications of a terminal. It was prepared by the Bryden group, which had also been very much involved in the development of the feasibility studies for the Weyburn terminal and therefore had experience in that regard. Before any final conclusion can be drawn, we have to analyse the total rail handling costs from that area into Churchill, alternative methods of gathering grain for Churchill, and also the question of the advantage in Churchill to the Wheat Board of having grain for sale there. As I indicated to the 42 or so farm and prairie organizations with whom I met to discuss this matter a few months ago, there is no doubt further work will continue, and no conclusions have been reached at this point.

subsubtopic: INLAND TERMINAL AT YORKTON, SASK-GOVERNMENT INTENTIONS REGARDING CONSTRUCTION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the fact of the matter is that this report came down on the side of no further expansion: it suggested no further expansion or improvement of the facilities at Churchill. Why would the minister take it upon himself to engage a consultant who had a very well known bias against the port of Churchill and who, in fact, did a study just two years ago for the Dominion Marine Association, which is pro-St. Lawrence Seaway, that recommended virtually the same situation; that the port of Churchill should not be expanded or improved? speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subsubtopic: INLAND TERMINAL AT YORKTON, SASK-GOVERNMENT INTENTIONS REGARDING CONSTRUCTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member's statement is really extraordinary. As a lawyer, he should know that a case may be taken for one side of a problem by a lawyer, and later on a case may be taken on the other side. Consultants operate in the same way. It is quite wrong for the hon. member to allege any kind of bias in the House on the part of any consultants. The fact of the matter is that in their work in relation to Churchill and in relation to inland terminals, they were knowledgeable about the entire situation.
As I said at the beginning, the hon. member is quite wrong in saying that this determined in some way that there was no future, or a dim future for Churchill. In fact, at this very moment we are continuing our programs of expansion for

Churchill. Lighting systems are being installed to allow longer hours of work at Churchill. This year we are likely to set again, for the third year in a row, a record for the number of bushels handled at Churchill. That is the record of this government. I do not know why the hon. member wants to be cynical about it.

speechtext:

Naturally I would like to express my appreciation to my colleagues in the Conservative caucus and to my solicitors, namely, from Brock-ville, the firm of Stewart, Corbett, Musclow and Barr, and my senior counsel here in Ottawa. subsubtopic: MR. COSSITT-NATIONAL SECURITY-DOCUMENT ALLEGED TO BE IN HON. MEMBER'S POSSESSION
speechtext:
I also feel that I should add, Mr. Speaker, before I read the reply to the House that I have given to the Solicitor General, that this whole incident has been extremely curious, and I consider it has been a breach of my parliamentary privilege.
It is an acknowledged fact that there are a number of members of this House who, at various times, have openly stated that they possess, or are quoting from so-called secret material, or from information given to them verbally. To my
Privilege-Mr. Cossitt
knowledge none of these members has been threatened with possible arrest. None of these members has been threatened with the issuance of search warrants. As a consequence, the question in my case I think is obvious-why have I been singled out by this government for the treatment I have received?
The conclusion is, 1 believe, just as obvious. I have never been exactly known as one who approves of the Prime Minister's (Mr. Trudeau) methods of running the country, and it would appear that the whole thing has become a form of some vindictive persecution on his part as evidenced by the threats made upon me last week in my office, without notice of any kind, by General Dare and the Solicitor General, on instructions that were apparently handed to the Solicitor General by the Prime Minister.
The Prime Minister has said that the interests of the country are at stake-as if I had damaged the interests of the country-but in reality I believe it is the interests of the government that are at stake in view of the fact that revelations made by a number of members in this House, including myself, have shown time and again the failure of the government to act decisively in the interests of national security.

subsubtopic: MR. COSSITT-NATIONAL SECURITY-DOCUMENT ALLEGED TO BE IN HON. MEMBER'S POSSESSION
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: MR. COSSITT-NATIONAL SECURITY-DOCUMENT ALLEGED TO BE IN HON. MEMBER'S POSSESSION

subsubtopic: MR. COSSITT-NATIONAL SECURITY-DOCUMENT ALLEGED TO BE IN HON. MEMBER'S POSSESSION
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: MR. COSSITT-NATIONAL SECURITY-DOCUMENT ALLEGED TO BE IN HON. MEMBER'S POSSESSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would now like to read to the House the letter dated March 3, 1978, delivered to me on that date at approximately 1.15 p.m. in the parliamentary dining room by a representative of the Solicitor General, along with my reply thereto.
80033-71/2

March 6, 1978
Privilege-Mr. Cossitt
The letter from the Solicitor General reads as follows:
Dear Sir:
I am satisfied that on the basis of statements made by you, both in and out of Parliament, that you are in possession of a document dated 24th March 1976, classified as 'Top Secret', entitled 'CANADIAN RELATED ACTIVITIES OF THE RUSSIAN INTELLIGENCE SERVICES' and published by the Intelligence Advisory Committee of the Government of Canada.
I am also satisfied that it would be prejudicial to the safety or interests of the State for you to retain possession of that official document. In the circumstances I consider it my duty as Solicitor General presiding over the Department of the Solicitor General to direct you, pursuant to the paragraph 4(4)(a) of the Official Secrets Act, to forthwith return the document together with any copies of it or extracts from it which you may have in your possession or which may be in the possession of others on your behalf.
You may be assured that this letter is being sent to you as a Member of Parliament only after my having given the matter very careful consideration and on my being absolutely convinced that it is necessary to do so in the interests of Canada.
I can be reached at any time through Government local 6-0220 or 2-4211.
Yours sincerely,
J.-J. Blais Solicitor General
The reply I have sent the Solicitor General across the floor of the House, dated this day, March 6, reads as follows:
Dear Mr. Blais:
I acknowledge receipt of your letter of March 3, 1978, which was delivered to me at approximately 1.15 p.m. on that date in the Parliamentary Dining Room shortly before my departure to my home in Brockville.
In response to your said letter I have to advise you that I am not in possession of a document dated March 24, 1976, classified as 'TOP SECRET', entitled 'CANADIAN RELATED ACTIVITIES OF THE RUSSIAN INTELLIGENCE SERVICES'.
Yours sincerely,
Tom Cossitt
In other words, or in effect, to summarize the wordiness of both letters, the Solicitor General has requested me to return forthwith a document classified as top secret and entitled "Canadian Related Activities of the Russian Intelligence Services" and I have replied to him that I am not in possession of such a document.

I have a notice from the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen) on a separate question of privilege.
To set this matter in its proper context, it was raised on Thursday and discussed further on Friday. When it was raised on Thursday it was raised as a result of a meeting that took place in the office of the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Cossitt) when the hon. Solicitor General (Mr. Blais) attended there in company with General Dare. At that time a conversation was held between the parties relating to documents that were allegedly in the possession of the hon. member for Leeds. At that time there was some indication that official action of some sort might be necessary by the Solicitor General.
When the point was raised by the hon. member for Leeds he brought to the attention of the House his request that he be permitted to consult counsel over the course of the weekend to determine what position he would take in respect to whatever documents about which he gave an undertaking. He gave an
Privilege-Mr. Nielsen
undertaking that any documents in his possession which would be of a certain nature would be held in safekeeping over the weekend by him. That was his undertaking. In response to this undertaking the matter was argued extensively Thursday afternoon. On Friday morning I spoke with both parties and it was agreed that the matter would stand over until Monday. That would not inhibit the serving of an official notice upon the hon. member for Leeds by the Solicitor General.
In respect therefore to one of such documents a notice was served. The response of the hon. member for Leeds this afternoon is that he is not in possession of the document described in that official notice. This disposes in a complete way of the question relating to that particular document and the hon. member's response to the notice served. It may leave open questions about other documents which might have been discussed on Thursday afternoon about which the hon. member for Leeds gave an undertaking of safekeeping during the weekend. I do not know. I have no information about the number of documents that are in his possession. However, it seems to me that the matter, having stood over in respect to any other documents at this time, cannot go any further in terms of procedural action by the Chair unless and until some other action is taken by one side or the other.
At this point, the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Cossitt) has raised by way of a question of privilege what is in effect his response to a specific notice under the Official Secrets Act, that is, a response to an official notice that the document is not in his possession. That may finalize that matter. It may also leave open the matters from Thursday with respect to other documents.
At the moment there is no procedural matter before the Chair for decision, and certainly no matter which has been formulated by the hon. member by way of a question of privilege that the Chair could deal with at this point. Whether or not that might arise in response to further action, now that this response by him has been made, is an open question. However, it is quite clear there is no action from a procedural point of view that the Chair can take at this moment.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to raise a separate question of privilege of which I have given Your Honour notice. I do so because of my increasing concern as an individual member of this House, which concern is shared generally by all members of the opposition, if not indeed by some on the other side of the House as well. It has to do with the coming into possession, the receiving of information in any form which might be classified as secret information under the Official Secrets Act.
Over the course of my years here I have come into possession of all sorts of that kind of information which could be so classified. It is quite obvious that other members on this side have as well. I know that I cannot get into the merits of my

March 6, 1978
Privilege-Mr. Nielsen
motion now, but I am just explaining what gives rise to my very deep concern about the extent to which that act is going to negate the responsibilities of members of parliament, particularly those in the opposition.
If that act were to be applied literally, we would have to place the telephone back in its cradle each time we made an assessment as to whether information we were hearing was classified.
Because of the importance of this question and the applicability of the Official Secrets Act to members of parliament, and because there has been a precedent set in the Mother of Parliaments in 1939 by way of a decision of a select committee, I believe it is urgently timely for this matter to be brought current in this place so that members of parliament, in their freedom of speech and their freedom to act in what they feel to be in the best interests of the state, for after all there are some of us who believe that the interests of the state and those of the government are not necessarily synonymous-

subtopic: MR. NIELSEN-APPLICABILITY OF OFFICIAL SECRETS ACT TO MEMBERS OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: MR. NIELSEN-APPLICABILITY OF OFFICIAL SECRETS ACT TO MEMBERS OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
Because of the urgent need to have this matter updated so that we can all feel free from arrest, free from search, and feel that we are fulfilling what are our responsibilities in this House, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Central Nova (Mr. MacKay), and these words are taken from the English precedent which is found in Beauchesne commencing at page 417:
That the applicability of the Official Secrets Act to members of the House in the discharge of their parliamentary duties, having regard to the undoubted privileges of the House as confirmed in Section 4 of the Senate of the House of Commons Act, Section 18 of the British North America Act and the ruling of Mr. Speaker of the House of Commons of Canada made on December 5, 1977 commencing at page 1539 of Hansard of that date and referring to the question of privilege raised by the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton commencing at page 935 of Hansard of November 16, 1977, be referred to the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections and to report back to this House within 30 days.

subtopic: MR. NIELSEN-APPLICABILITY OF OFFICIAL SECRETS ACT TO MEMBERS OF PARLIAMENT

The hon. member gave the Chair notice of his question of privilege and now follows it with a substantive motion. I would, in an initial way, have a very grave reservation about any attempt to raise by way of a question of privilege a general proposition which is not founded on a particular case. Particularly do I say so in respect to a situation which appears to parallel another event that appears, at least for the moment, not to have reached its final conclusion.
In addition, I would want to remark to the House that a committee was established, under my chairmanship, of which the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) was very much the inspiration, as a special committee of the House on the question of the rights and immunities of members. It has made one report to the House and it has taken under consideration a number of equally important matters.
I want to give some consideration overnight to whether or not the proper resolution of this would be to refer, or at least request that committee, since it has already the authority of the House to study a number of matters affecting rights and

immunities, to priorize this subject as its next report to the House, if at all possible within the time available, and to take into account events that are unfolding at the present time as well as all of the items referred to here.
That would, I hope, accomplish the same thing in an equally effective way and would not offend the proposition that the matter is really of too general a nature to found a question of privilege on the basis of the precedents, but it is certainly an important enough matter to be given immediate attention. subtopic: MR. NIELSEN-APPLICABILITY OF OFFICIAL SECRETS ACT TO MEMBERS OF PARLIAMENT

Mr. Speaker, in view of the comments by the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen) to the effect that he would hope that submissions might be made tomorrow on the matter of his motion, presumably to prove that his motion raises a prima facie case of privilege, I want to say at this point that I vigorously submit that this motion does not present a prima facie case of privilege in any way, shape, or form.
It could be a substantive motion that the hon. member could put on the order paper and have dealt with in that way. However, it is worth recalling to the House that Your Honour has already ruled that whatever question of privilege or alleged question of privilege has been raised by the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Cossitt), either on Thursday or today, has been discharged. To put it another way, it has not been put forward in any way that it could constitute a proceeding of the House. I therefore take it that that episode, in so far as privilege is concerned, is closed in the way that it has been dealt with today.
The hon. member for Yukon is raising the very general question of the relationship of the Official Secrets Act to members of parliament. It is a very general proposition that is of great academic interest. However, it is not related to any question of privilege or any grievance, breach or complaint put forward by any member of parliament, not even the hon. member for Yukon. The hon. member for Yukon has not said that he has been imperilled or held back in the discharge of his duties because of the operation of the Official Secrets Act.
Having said that with regard to the motion, it seems to me that the suggestion Your Honour has made is an eminently sensible one, to have the committee which has already constituted itself regard this as an appropriate matter for priority
March 6, 1978

treatment. It would certainly have my support and the support of members on this side of the House if it were dealt with on a basis of priority with no motion or further action required on the part of the House.
I believe it is essential that we deal with this matter so that we can go on to the allotted day and deal with the matter standing before the House in the name of the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby (Mr. Broadbent).

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: MR. NIELSEN-APPLICABILITY OF OFFICIAL SECRETS ACT TO MEMBERS OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I quite agree with the statements made by the government House leader with respect to the necessity of proceeding with the allotted day. However, I must say I am very heartened to hear two things.
The first is the importance which Your Honour attaches to the question of the relationship of the rights of a member of parliament and the Official Secrets Act, particularly with regard to the way in which a member of parliament can perform his duties and what limitations there may be on him. I am very pleased with the suggestion you have made and the idea of priorizing that in the Committee on Rights and Immunities which is chaired by Your Honour. That makes it even more important. I was very pleased to hear that suggestion.
I was particularly pleased to hear the approbation and endorsation of the suggestion by the government House leader. This is a matter of extreme importance, one with which all of us should be concerned. I want to thank the hon. member for that suggestion.

subtopic: MR. NIELSEN-APPLICABILITY OF OFFICIAL SECRETS ACT TO MEMBERS OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to lend my support to the idea which has been put forward by yourself and endorsed by the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. MacEachen) and, now, by the official opposition as well. However, in resolving the matter at this point by a reference to the Committee on Rights and Immunities, under Your Honour's chairmanship, we should be clear in our minds about what the committee would be looking into.
As I see it, this is a matter which not only affects the rights and privileges of members of parliament and the security of the country as they relate to the Official Secrets Act but also a specifically related question, which is the limits, if any, which should be placed on the right of a member not to divulge his source of information. This is a fundamental question and one which has concerned members on both sides in this unfortunate circumstance-if I may use that adjective to describe it- the rather heavy-handed action taken by the government before the week end, an action which was justified, in the view of the administration, not on the assumption that it was necessary to obtain the information in the document or documents alleged to be in the hands of the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Cossitt) but because the obtaining of that document or documents would be an important step in getting to the source of the leak. It was this-the question of sources which I took to be the essence of the government's interest at the time, and
Privilege-Mr. Nielsen
I also took it to be the essence of the interest of the hon. member for Leeds.
There is involved here a fundamental dilemma in a parliamentary democracy-the right of an hon. member on either side of the House to protect his or her sources of information. I need not only draw attention to the case dealt with in Great Britain, to which reference was made early this afternoon; a similar matter was before the Ontario legislature in recent months.
The committee over which Your Honour presides is particularly suited to deal with such a matter, not only because of the nature of the subject matter but in terms of its composition- its members are admirably suited to deal with such a reference. They include the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin), the hon. member for Richmond (Mr. Beaudoin), the hon. member for Windsor West (Mr. Gray), the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), the hon. member for Saint-Denis (Mr. Prud'homme), and the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Reid). These members have shown by their past interest in such matters that they are admirably suited to deal with this question. They have shown an understanding of what is at the root of the problem, namely, the rights of members of parliament as opposed to, or in comparison with, the rights and responsibilities of the executive branch.
What is so perturbing is that the heavy-handed action of the government just prior to the week end revealed that the government-I am inclined to say this would apply to any government of the day, including one from my own party-is inclined to define national security in terms of its own party policy. If you hold power it is almost inescapable that, in national security matters, you will identify the security of the state with the policy of your own government. When such a situation arises and power is exercised in terms of a set of options, including the possibility of arrest, being presented to a member of parliament, serious questions are raised about the propriety of the executive branch of the government making a judgment in its own case, a judgment which possibly impinges upon the rights of that member. We find the government interpreting and applying the Official Secrets Act and saying, with regard to its own case, "This is a threat to the security of the state," and so on.
In this case the difficulty is compounded by the role which has been actively played by the hon. member for Leeds. To no one's surprise, and, many will think to his credit, he has zeroed in on the activities of the Prime Minister of the day (Mr. Trudeau). I am not passing judgment on that, but he certainly has done so. So when the government, through its power as the executive branch, decides to bring down the law of the state on a member, we have to keep in mind that in this instance we are not talking about an academic or hypothetical situation but about a very real one. The government, defining its own defence policy from a set of regulations, has equated it with the national interest, and the situation is not made easier by the fact that many of the activities of the hon. member concerned have been directed against the Prime Minister.

March 6, 1978
Privilege-Mr. Nielsen
However, what is involved fundamentally in this issue is not the obtaining of documents for their own sake but getting to the source of the leak. This brings up the question of the rights of members of parliament. It is not the case, as was said by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang), that an hon. member has the same rights and privileges as any other citizen of Canada, and no more. We have added rights and privileges. For example, we can say things here in this chamber which, if said outside it, would be in violation of the law of libel. We have freedom here to criticize the government to an extent which, outside the House, would be described as licence.
To my mind the basic question is this: if we are to exercise our rights as members of parliament to express ourselves freely, to be vigorous critics of the government, if we are in opposition, or vigorous backbench members on the other side, it is of the highest importance that we protect our sources of information, especially when such information is frequently volunteered. I might say it is inevitable that it should be volunteered in a free society. This being the case, the question to be considered by the committee is: when that right to protect sources of information is weighed against the security of the state, where does one come down? Because 1 do not believe the executive branch is the authority which should decide that question, I support the proposal to refer the matter to the consideration of a committee of this House, the committee chaired by Your Honour. The committee would look at this possible conflict of rights or obligations, and weigh a member's right to information, and right to protect his sources, against the right of the state to maintain security.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: MR. NIELSEN-APPLICABILITY OF OFFICIAL SECRETS ACT TO MEMBERS OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is nothing more important to members of parliament and to freedom itself than the maintenance of the basic principle that members of parliament do not have to reveal the source of their information. The Leader of the NDP (Mr. Broadbent) has dealt with that and I want to deal with it on the basis of experience.
Having been Prime Minister I know that matters arise that are prejudicial to government. Governments are human, and when matters like that arise, naturally they find a variety of opinions in order to offset the right of parliament. I will now quote the Sandys case. I know Sandys very well. He is today a member of the House of Lords, the son-in-law of Sir Winston Churchill. The view that he expressed on parliamentary privilege is as clear today as when he uttered these words. He relied, among other things, on expressions in the Economist of July 2, 1938, in the following passage:
It is imperative even in a democracy that certain facts which might be helpful to a possible enemy should be kept secret. The government must be accorded adequate powers to ensure that, in such cases, this secrecy is safeguarded. But it is equally essential, both for the safety of the state and for the preservation of liberty, that the House of Commons and the press should not be hampered in exercising their traditional right-which is also their duty-of criticism. This function can only be effectively performed if members of parliament and journalists are well informed; hence it is part of their day-to-day business to secure information from all possible sources.
I do not place members of the press on the same level as members of parliament, nor do they themselves, but the fact remains that when governments do not want information to be made available to the people that may be prejudicial to them, often they assert it is prejudicial to the state. That is the danger, and once it is accepted that a government can say that a member of parliament shall reveal his sources of informa-
March 6, 1978

tion, freedom ends, because no one could communicate, no matter how serious the allegation the individual has in mind, if he realizes it would be revealed. It cannot be, it dare not be. We in this parliament accept that principle.
If the individual should be named and the information given so that all who read the information may understand who it was, parliament might as well close down. Information is received over and over again; it has to be checked to ascertain whether it is well based. Often the information that is sent in is allegedly reputable and dependable, but it turns out not to be such. What has happened in the present case is that the Government of Canada, through the Solicitor General (Mr. Blais), and the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), would place members of parliament in a position of being in pawn to them. That cannot be accepted by parliament if this institution is to be preserved.

subtopic: MR. NIELSEN-APPLICABILITY OF OFFICIAL SECRETS ACT TO MEMBERS OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: MR. NIELSEN-APPLICABILITY OF OFFICIAL SECRETS ACT TO MEMBERS OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
I mentioned my own experience. On one occasion it was said that it was a breach of the Official Secrets Act, to which I said, "Possibly, technically, and maybe", but the principle of the independence of parliament does not permit any government to say to any member, "You shall only speak what we want to accept, and you shall only speak what we believe is within the provisions of the Official Secrets Act".
Mr. Speaker, you have a tremendous responsibility in this. The determination of the course to be followed is one that rests with you. The preservation of our prerogative rights, the maintenance of the principles on which parliament is founded now rest with you in view of the acceptance today of the authority which you are prepared to accept, and I ask you, in the interests of this parliament, of this generation, and of generations to come, that you do not follow the request of the Government of Canada which, in effect, would place members of parliament in the position of being subservient to them, permitting the government to determine what is or is not within the regulations on the defence of Canada.
I do not want to belabour the point unnecessarily, but let me say that not since John Wilkes took his stand, and Duncan Sandys took his stand in 1938, as I have already mentioned, has any speaker in Canada been placed in the position in which Your Honour finds yourself, as the custodian and protector of the rights of the parliament of this country.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-EQUALITY OF RIGHTS FOR WOMEN IN LABOUR FORCE
speechtext:
That this House asserts that the women of Canada ought to have fully equal rights in participating in the Canadian economy, and in relation thereto condemns the government for its discriminatory policies and statements regarding Canadian women in the labour force.
He said: Mr. Speaker, as leader of the New Democratic Party I have spoken many times about unemployment and its effects on the economy of our country and on every working as well as non-working Canadian. I have tried, particularly over the last two years, to get the Liberal government to provide economic opportunities for Canadians to work. Canadians
March 6, 1978

want the opportunity to work, they do not want to go on collecting handouts of one kind or another.
The opportunity to work is not only important because of its relationship to human dignity and what it means to be a human being, but also in terms of its net effect on the economy. When you have more than 1 million unemployed we lose millions of tax dollars that would otherwise be collected, and we lose the production of millions of dollars worth of goods and services that are not being produced. We also pay out, as we are now paying, some $4 billion a year in unemployment insurance. Unemployment, in short, is a major problem for both human and economic reasons.
As I have said, until today I have talked in the House of Commons about unemployment in general terms. Today I want to talk about what I call the forgotten victims of our unemployment, and I refer to the Canadian women. All of us in and outside this House at this point in our history are aware of such recent economic happenings as the lay-off of men by Inco in Sudbury, and at Thompson, Manitoba, and the shutdown by Alcan of its operations at St. Lawrence, Newfoundland. A few days ago in the House of Commons we learned of another shutdown of a mining operation in Stewart, British Columbia.
Few members of parliament are aware that Canadian women are greater victims of unemployment and the resultant poor economic situation than are men. 1 regret to say that most members of parliament still tend to think of men as being the only breadwinners in our society. That happens to be a reality in terms of the perceptions of most hon. members. Like so many beliefs about our economy and unemployment, this is a myth. It is a myth to believe that men are the only breadwinners in our present economy. I say that because more and more Canadian families require two incomes to survive in 1978, with the cost of living rising month after month, year after year.
Canadian women, who are the subject of this debate, work in the main for the same reasons as Canadian men. They work to buy groceries, to pay fuel bills, to buy clothes for their children, and to pay the mortgages on their homes. They work for the same reasons that their husbands work: to meet the necessities of life in Canada. Approximately one half of married women who are working are doing so because otherwise their husbands, children, and families would be at the poverty level. That is the reality of working wives in 1978.
The women working in fish plants in St. John's or working as cab drivers in Ottawa, such as the ones I spoke with not long ago, are frequently putting in 8, 10, 12 or 14 hour days, rather than the normal eight hour day. This is the case with many women who are doing various ordinary jobs throughout the breadth of this country. They are putting in these long hours fo; the same reasons as men in similar situations. It is not to buy a fur coat, nor to have the advantage of an extra bit of material well-being. They are doing it to meet the necessity
Status of Women
of living from day to day in Canada. That is why they are working.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-EQUALITY OF RIGHTS FOR WOMEN IN LABOUR FORCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-EQUALITY OF RIGHTS FOR WOMEN IN LABOUR FORCE
speechtext:
I am not referring just to married women. This debate has to be also concerned about the plight of single women. They are an important part of our society as well. And they are an important part of the Canadian economy today. In addition to the working wives, there are more than l'/2 million single women working to earn a living. Among that V/2 million, 200,000 women are the sole support of their families. I am referring to the single parent families, which are increasing in number. They are the widows, the divorced, and the deserted. That is what makes up the 200,000 single parent households in this country. I want to stress that most of these women are working at wages which are not equal to nor in excess of those of men. In most cases they are working at wages which are below the poverty level. That is the situation with which working single women are faced.
At the outset of my comments, I said that the majority of women who are unemployed in Canada have become the forgotten victims of unemployment. That is not simply a bit of self-indulgent rhetoric. 1 assert that because it is a statistical reality. If one includes in the statistical unemployment figures all the men and women who would take jobs if they were available and possible, instead of the almost one million unemployed Canadians which Statistics Canada indicates, the real figure is 1.6 million. That part of our labour market, which includes men and women who are no longer in the official statistics but want work, can be referred to as the hidden unemployed. Among that almost countless number, who are not referred to in the official statistics, more than 700,000 women would like to have jobs, need work, but cannot get it. If these are included the real rate of unemployment for last month for women was 17 per cent. A government which was at all sensitive to human issues would consider that to be a statistical scandal. Just as the government tried originally many months ago to deny the existence and significance of the category of hidden unemployed, now it is attempting to hide the reality of the women within that category, whom I call the forgotten unemployed.
Not merely is the government ignoring the myths which are still prevalent in some circles concerning working women in the economy, unbelievably the government and its ministers are perpetuating those myths. In its manpower retraining programs and unemployment insurance offices it is actively discriminating against women. At this point in the twentieth century, surely that should be totally unacceptable to a civilized government.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-EQUALITY OF RIGHTS FOR WOMEN IN LABOUR FORCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-EQUALITY OF RIGHTS FOR WOMEN IN LABOUR FORCE
speechtext:
1 realize the minister responsible for the status of women will join in the debate this afternoon. Hon. members on this side of the House will listen with a great deal of interest. For the minister's benefit I should like to refer to some information that comes from the Advisory Council on

March 6, 1978
Status of Women
the Status of Women, which was responsible to his department. I refer to its annual report for 1976-1977 regarding the government's activities vis-a-vis women in government departments. Page 9 indicates that the last report revealed in the area of salaries that men were still far ahead of women, and that there had been a decrease in the number of women in senior executive positions.
In addition, the study noted that the concentration of women in certain job categories was even more marked. For example, more than three quarters of the administrative support positions are now filled by women, compared to only 68 per cent in 1974, which is the year the government launched its equal opportunities program. Those figures indicate the progress of that program. Under the category of appointments of women, over which the government and its ministers exercise complete authority, the report of that council is a very unhappy one. It indicates that the government has not lived up to the promises made some years ago in this regard. I will not quote at length from the report in that respect.
For the benefit of the minister, I should like to refer to the case of Miss Ritchie. I am sure all hon. members are aware of it. She served with distinction, skill, and indeed reforming zeal as vice-chairman of the Anti-Dumping Tribunal for the past five years. When the position of chairman became vacant, it was not offered to her in recognition of the outstanding job she did. The position was given to a man. There are many examples within government agencies to which I could refer. I should like to refer to one other instance which took place in my constituency.
Last October a young woman in my riding wrote to me. She was a distinguished high school student. She wanted to become a pilot in the air force. She had contacted the appropriate depot in Toronto to apply. She was surprised to learn in 1977-that is when it occured-that she would not be eligible. Why? Because she was a woman. She knew at the time that in other countries progress had been made in this respect. She knew that there were Russian astronauts who were women. She knew that the Americans were admitting female cadets to West Point and that the Americans were training pilots who were not exclusively male but included women.
I wrote to the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Danson) in this regard. Just the other day I received in reply a three-page single spaced letter. I knew why it was so long. I knew he was weasling his way to the conclusion of the letter and that at the end of the letter the minister would say that this young woman from my constituency would not be admitted to train as a pilot. Sure enough, that was the conclusion. There were a number of reasons given, most of them bad, but the one which offended me most was the assertion that the Americans were conducting experiments in this area. So, said the Minister of National Defence in reply to me, and the implication is clear: we will see what happens with the American experience, and if it turns out all right, it will be good enough for Canada. Surely that is not good enough. Are there

not some areas in which a Liberal government can have enough courage and show enough imagination to lead instead of following American examples?
In terms of his department's obligations the Minister of National Defence is by no means alone in discriminating against women. The Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Cullen) is in a category all by himself in this respect. Both he and the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) have been reported, not once but several times, as blaming youth and women for high unemployment rates in Canada. Specifically, a couple of weeks ago the Minister of Employment and Immigration said that the government, along with Liberal backbenchers, should explain unemployment away in 1978 with this little piece of euphemistic nonsense from a statement prepared by him:
Unemployment no longer means what it used to-loss of all family income. Close to two thirds of the unemployed are in families with at least one other wage earner. In fact, over half the beneficiaries are secondary or tertiary wage earners.
That is from the gospel according to the Minister of Employment and Immigration. That is myth No. 1 which the government is trying not to correct but to perpetuate. The myth is that unemployment among married women does not really matter because they are secondary earners. Another interpretation of the same quotation is that if a husband loses his job, that too does not matter because his working partner can still be there to bring home the bacon. That is classic twisted and deceptive Liberal logic.
The reality is that 4 million working women today make up 40 per cent of the work force in Canada. They are not some marginal part of the Canadian economy. They are a major part, 40 per cent. The reality is that almost one half of them are not secondary wage earners at all but are the sole providers either for themselves or their families.
Of the 200,000 single parents with dependent children for whom we had statistics in 1975-and they are the most recent statistics-one half had incomes of less than $5,000, which is less than the poverty level. However, what about the married woman, the secondary earner to whom the Minister of Employment and Immigration callously refers? As I asked rhetorically earlier, is she working to get a holiday in some southern climate, to buy a fur coat, or to buy a new sports car? Of course not. As I pointed out earlier, she is working to buy essential requirements for her family. The $5,000 to $6,000 working wives typically earn in no way can be construed as mere pin money. These people are not buying frills. They are buying the essentials of human life.
I want to deal now with myth No. 20. We hear it not only in conversations around this chamber; we also hear it, I regret to say, from time to time in all our constituencies in all parts of Canada. The myth is that women are causing unemployment among men. Both the Minister of Employment and Immigration and the Prime Minister have referred a number of times to the allegation that increasing participation of women in the labour force has caused a recent growth in unemployment.
March 6, 1978

What are the facts? Between 1967 and 1977 the participation rate for women increased by 25 per cent, but the unemployment rate for men and women during the same period of time increased by 100 per cent. Even a Liberal economist should be able to understand the meaning of those figures. The meaning is that women coming onto the labour market are not creating unemployment among men. It is not only nonsense but cruel nonsense to blame women for doing so. However, the most alarming statistic in this regard is that for the past decade, while the participation rate for women increased by 25 per cent, their unemployment level went from 3.7 per cent to 9.5 per cent, an increase of 300 per cent over that period of time. That is a much greater increase than the increase in the rate of unemployment for men. No, Mr. Speaker, women have not been taking jobs away from men. I hope the minister who replies will deal with these issues.
Let us consider the occupations of most women in our country. The reality is that two thirds of women workers are in clerical, sales or service jobs. What is particularly significant about these jobs in the context of the argument that women are taking employment away from men? Almost all of them were rejected a long time ago by men, principally for the reason that the wages are lower than men consider to be acceptable. Those are the kinds of jobs most women still have in our society. I want to give some figures in that regard because they are important, and they are part of our attempt to document this problem. They are drawn from 1975 statistics again.
The average wage level in service occupations was $4,711. The average wage in sales occupations was $5,545. For clerical work the average wage was $7,157. The reality is that women are not stealing men's jobs at all. The reality is that they are still being held down to the lowest paying jobs in our society which, by and large, men have rejected. To twist this reality inside out by accusing women of taking men's jobs is simply to heap cruelty upon injustice. I say that to the government in all seriousness.
In the debate this afternoon I have used a number of statistics. More could have been brought forward to deepen the criticism of the government, but I will not do that. Other contributors to this debate will have an opportunity to add to that. I have used these statistics to portray through this forum to the people of Canada the picture of the economic reality for Canadian women.
I have attempted to present statistical hard core information which I hope will go some way to correct the myths which the government not only has allowed to persist but has perpetuated by its action, on the one hand, and by its inaction on the other.
I do not normally like to use personal examples in debate but, like many members of this House, I have both a son and a daughter. I have a son who is 18 years old and a daughter who has just turned five. What is so important to me is that my daughter as well as my son should have the opportunity and the expectation of not only a decent home, a decent retirement pension plan, but also a decent job. As a woman she should have that right.
Status of Women
So, Mr. Speaker, I say to you that it is time the government came to grips in general with the problem of unemployment for all the 1.6 million who are unemployed but, most specifically today, I say that in addressing ourselves at long last in parliament to the problems of unemployment, we should keep in mind that the dreams of Canadian women have a full and equal place in the scheme of things with the dreams of Canadian men.

I should like to put on the record in general terms some of the things done by this government in the last few years.

I would like to say that we, as a government, are proud of what we have done to improve the status of women in Canada in the last ten years. Long before governments of the western world started to concern themselves with this matter, the government of Canada, under the administration of the Hon. Lester B. Pearson, appointed an inquiry commission which gave us a blueprint under the basis of which we developed a comprehensive policy in this field, and we did not wait for International Women's Year to examine this question. Mr. Speaker, this royal commission submitted 122 recommendations to the federal government and the great majority, or about 98, have already been completely or partly implemented through legislative amendments or administrative changes.
Ours was also the first government of the western world to appoint a minister specifically responsible for the status of women in 1971. This was the Minister of Labour (Mr. Munro). Ours was the first government in Canada to create an independent advisory council on the status of women. Ours is the only government in the country to have established a responsibility center within the government, the Office of the Status of Women Coordinator. Moreover, much progress has been made to give women equal treatment before the law and to eliminate any discrimination, and I can give a few examples of this: the omnibus bill of 1975 to amend the Immigration Act, the Public Service Employment Act, the Unemployment Insurance Act, and the Canadian Labour Code, the amendments to the Canadian Citizenship Act, under which either parent can transmit citizenship and which were promulgated in February 1977, the 1976 amendments to the Criminal Code

which amended the procedure in case of rape and increased the protection of women's rights.
Finally, we amended the Canada Pension Plan to guarantee the equality of status of contributors and beneficiaries of both sexes in 1975. There is also the amendment that provides for the possibility of sharing non-adjusted gains of a contributor in the case of divorce or annulment of marriage which was adopted in 1978. We wanted to go further in this amendment to the Canada Pension Plan so as not to penalize any person who must leave the labour force to raise children, but the Ontario government refused to co-operate in this regard.
And last, we had recently the Human Rights Act forbidding discrimination based on sex and family situation and salary differences between men and women doing similar work. [English]
These are the steps that have been taken by this government in the last ten years. Just before that there was the creation of the Royal Commission on the Status of Women, and out of the 122 recommendations the commission made, 98 were implemented entirely or partially.
This is the first government in the western world to appoint a minister especially responsible for the status of women. This is the first government in Canada to create an Advisory Council on the Status of Women. We have been presenting amending legislation to this House year after year to eliminate discrimination in all our legislation, making sure that legal equality is guaranteed to women as well as to men.
We have amended the Citizenship Act, the Canada Pensions Act and the Criminal Code with respect to the status of women. But we have also acted in the area of appointment. The Leader of the New Democratic Party made a passing reference to this. I would like to point out that under the present Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) we are the first party to have elected eight women to parliament, in the last election.
We are the first government to have three outstanding women in the cabinet. We are the first government to have appointed a woman lieutenant governor, and we are the first government to have appointed a woman as an associate chief justice in this country.
The hon. member has referred to the Anti-Dumping Tribunal. I could refer him to the Tariff Board. In that instance we went outside to appoint a woman as president of that board over the head of a competent man who was a vice-chairman.

At the federal level we are very anxious to remove the last remnant of discrimination based on sex and still found in the Indian Act. We are committed to ensuring that the views of all Indian women are considered in discussions we are having with the National Indian Brotherhood. We will be giving the Indian Rights for Indian Women group some funds to enable them to have some input into this process which is taking place.
We still need to look at divorce legislation, income tax legislation, sexual offences in the Criminal Code, the position of women in the Armed Forces, and further means of helping women in the labour force and those who remain at home.
In order to have a fresh look at these and other questions which are of interest to women we have decided to develop a plan of action or global policy on the status of women. This will detail both legislation and practice necessary to achieve concrete goals between now and 1985, the end of the international decade for women. We have had initial discussions with the provinces on this question and we hope that many of them will be reviewing their own policies and programs with a view to responding to the needs of their citizens.
As far as we are concerned, there are 25 government departments and about 100 officials who are involved in a complete review of all recommendations made to the government in all areas under its jurisdiction.
Under the motion, the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby has accused the government of "discriminatory policies and state-
Status of Women
ments regarding Canadian women in the labour force". In fact this was the theme of a speech which he gave in Toronto on February 19, 1978. He stated that the government was trying to hide the reality of unemployment among women and that "instead of doing the appropriate job of exploding myths, the government is perpetuating them".
Well, I would like to respond to the charge of the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby by quoting from the text of a speech that I gave to the federal-provincial territorial meeting on the status of women in Ottawa on February 16, 1978, which was reported in the media. This is what I had to say:
The growing weight of evidence points to the fact that women are entering the labour force for the same reasons as men-out of a need for self-realization and in order to maintain themselves and their families. Close to half of the three million women in the work force support themselves or others. More than one third are single. Another 10 per cent are widowed, divorced or separated. Recent studies indicate that more and more families are basing their standard of living on two incomes. A Statistics Canada study on income inequality suggests that in the growing number of families with two wage earners, employed wives play a considerable role in alleviating financial hardship, and to a lesser extent, poverty. These facts explode the myth that all women are secondary wage earners.
Clearly the government is not trying to hide the problems that unemployment poses for women in the labour force. If anything we are trying to make Canadians aware of the reasons behind the entry of women into the work force. On this point my remarks obviously succeeded in raising the consciousness of the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby, since three days later he echoed them in his speech.
What is happening in the economy? The hon. member referred to it in some parts of his speech. Since 1966 the Canadian labour force has increased by 37 per cent due to population growth, immigration, and rising participation rates. There has been a steady increase in the labour force participation rates of women of all ages, and adult women in particular. In the period between 1966 and 1976 the Canadian labour force participation rate of women rose from roughly 34 per cent to 45 per cent with the greatest increase in that age group often termed "prime age", that is, the age group between 25 and 44. The participation rate of adult women alone increased by 59 per cent over the same period and contributed significantly to the over-all labour force increase. In aggregate terms the economy responded well to the demands of women for employment. Employment growth among adult women relative to their population as compared to that among youth and adult males increased strongly over the last ten years.
As I pointed out, women have been entering the labour force not just out of a need for self-fulfilment, which is valid in itself, but increasingly for economic reasons to support themselves and their families. Whereas in the past women tended to enter the labour force during good times and drop out during bad times, their persistent high participation rates suggest that women in the work force are a phenomenon that is here to stay. This clearly invalidates the concept that all women are working for frills, as if they all had a "prime age male" to support them. We did not invent the "secondary wage earner" concept that economists use to describe the presence of women in the work place, nor are we stuck to it. Women want to, need to and, most importantly, have a right to work, and I agreed

What is important to recall, however, is that this is not something that can be done by the federal government alone. The federal parliament has authority over about only 10 per cent of the work force in this country. That implies that the provincial governments have large responsibilities over the work force also, and in a free country there are various voluntary organizations that are involved. This obviously implies the participation and the responsibility of the provincial governments as well as the federal government. It also involves a large role for the unions. I would like to pay tribute here to the women leaders of the labour movement such as Shirley Clark and Grace Hartman.

There is clearly a large task to be completed in the area of institutional change and change of attitude. For example, this implies action in the school system. What about the lack of appreciation by the school system, particularly for girls, of the benefits of working in industry and the necessity for our educational system to give more attention and more importance to training of women for the types of jobs they may later be called upon to perform?
We have been trying to act at the level of the public service. This is an area for which we, as a government, are directly responsible. This covers a large number of employees. It is quite clear that a lot still remains to be done in this area, but I would like to stress that the government has taken steps within the law and within the limits provided by the Public Service Employment Act and the autority of the Public Service Commission to try to improve opportunities for women in the public service.

I should like indeed to bring to your attention measures taken in November 1975 for instance, when guidelines were issued by the cabinet and government departments were given

the main responsibility for developing action programs to reach the objectives of the government, and I quote:
That within a reasonable period of time, the distribution of men and women within the public service by department, occupational groups and levels be proportional to the number of available, interested and competent employees of both sexes.
And for fiscal year 1977-78, on top of their annual program, the various departments had to develop long term programs, that is five year programs and measurable objectives. A study of data contained in the annual reports of the Public Service Commission shows that the percentage of women is slowly increasing in all occupational groups except in the scientific and professional category, where it remains the same. It is in the administrative and external service category that we can note the higher increase concerning the representation as well as the global distribution of women.

Steps have been taken. In 1975 directives were issued to departments to ensure that they had clear plans with regard to the promotion of women. It was insisted that they provide a five year plan to Treasury Board, showing their plan of action vis-a-vis their promotion of women. These are two very important steps to ensure that women are provided real equality of opportunity in the public service.
These plans have begun to show some results. Obviously one cannot go as fast as one would like. We are dealing here with people occupying jobs, collective agreements, and a system in the public service which everyone supports, the merit system. Quite clearly one cannot expect dramatic changes from year to year. What is important is that the trend being established is a positive one. It is quite clearly established by the statistics that have been published and made available up until this time.
While we have dealt with the promotion of women in the public service and on boards and commissions, we have also taken into consideration, in areas other than legislation, the needs of women across this country. Specifically, we have made funds available to women's groups across this country so that they might be better organized and to enable them to participate more fully in Canada's economic development. We are the only government in this country that has set aside special funds for this purpose. Some provinces will fund certain services traditionally viewed as women's services such as day care centres. However, not one government gives funds to women's organizations.
To what kinds of projects am I referring? During International Women's Year we allocated $5 million to enable the women of Canada to become aware of and knowledgeable about all the issues of concern to them.
The Secretary of State's women's program has had $500,000 every year for the last three or four years to fund projects of interest to women across the country. In that same department $300,000 is set aside every year for the funding of native women's programs. As the minister responsible for the status of women, I have a small fund which has been increased this year from $75,000 to $90,000. It enables grants to be given to
March 6, 1978

national women's organizations for various activities that they might undertake. What have these been used for?
[ Translation]
The Quebec Women Federation for instance has organized seminars and meetings to make Quebec women more aware of the political decision making process and encourage them to get more involved in politics and stand as candidates in municipal, provincial or federal elections-the fluency of the minister in both official languages.

In British Columbia a conference on women and economic development was held in November, 1977. Women from 42 single industry resource communities met to study the impact of economic development on women. In several parts of the country, workshops have been held. Public education programs have been organized. Newsletters have been published and annual meetings have been organized. All this is thanks to the federal funds.
In conclusion, while this issue has finally been raised at this late stage of this parliament, I wish to remind hon. members opposite that while they may be just awakening to the problems of women in the labour force, women themselves have long been taking the initiative to overcome these problems.
The National Action Committee on the Status of Women will be meeting in Ottawa in mid-March to discuss women and the economy. Women are also giving a great deal of attention to the choices girls of 12 and 13 make when they enter high school, for they know that all too often the choice of a commercial course will limit those girls to a lifetime of low-paid, clerical support work. Women themselves are addressing the fundamental questions, and have been doing so for well over the past decade.
Women know, only too well, that there are no short-cuts to gaining equality. We wish there were, but there are not. Women are not impressed by the new found lip service that members of the opposition are hatching in order to try to show their latter-day opportunistic concern for women.
