speechtext: Even though the minister chose not to deal with the substance of the motion before us, I wish to do so. The two fundamental points made clear in the motion put forward by the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby are, first, that we continue to be a country where there is not equality in fact for the women of Canada and, second, that this condition becomes seriously and dangerously aggravated when we have serious economic problems such as we are facing at the present time. The women of Canada are the first to suffer when the economy is in decline; they are the first to suffer when unemployment is as acute as it is in this country now. Any government which refuses to recognize this fact, which refuses to take the opportunity to get the economy rolling, deserves the support of neither the women nor the men who comprise the electorate and citizenry of Canada.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-EQUALITY OF RIGHTS FOR WOMEN IN LABOUR FORCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-EQUALITY OF RIGHTS FOR WOMEN IN LABOUR FORCE
speechtext:
I was amused to hear the minister talk about the degree to which women themselves are addressing the subject of the status of women. There has never been any question about that. We did not need the editorial comment of the minister to know about it. The sad fact is that while women have been addressing their problems and doing what they can, the one entity in Canada which has the power to change the laws of Canada is the Government of Canada and it has done very very little to help women in their task. That is the reason for this motion; that is the reason for the consistent concern of those of us who intend to form the next government in Canada to put on the agenda of this country and of this parliament some of the specific reforms which we want to act on very quickly. We want to see that women no longer have to put up with recycled speeches from that minister, but will instead have an agenda for action which we in my party propose, by an amendment later today, to introduce onto the floor of the House of Commons.
The Leader of the New Democratic Party and the minister referred to some of the very real problems which exist for Canadian women. I want to deal with two of the myths which I believe, regretfully, have been put forward by members of the government in trying to defend themselves for not taking action to stimulate the Canadian economy in an attempt to defend the indefensible.
More than a million Canadians are out of work. We are in an economy in which we do not know how many more people would enter the work force were there an active work force for them to enter. Particularly do I refer to women. But two very vicious myths are now in circulation. One of those is that working women take jobs which would otherwise be taken by men. Another is that many of the women who work in this country do so simply as a luxury, not because they need to do so but simply because they want to-as if that were not reason enough. I want to deal with those two aspects if I may, first, the myth that married women take jobs from married men who have families to support. The statistics are clear.
In 1977 there were 2,212,000 married women in the Canadian labour force. In 1977 212,000 married men were unem-
[Mr. Clark.l
ployed. The fact is clear from those two figures that if married women stopped working two million jobs would be unfilled.
One of the points is the types of jobs to which Canadian women are too often confined. Although the number of women in the Canadian labour force is increasing, the types of jobs that they are doing have changed very little. The kinds of jobs are traditionally those of secretaries, nurses, tellers, teachers or clerks. These remain basically unchanged, and this underlines the point that simply decreasing the number of women in the labour force will not significantly help the unemployment situation for men in Canada. The jobs which would be vacated by women getting out of the labour force are certainly not the jobs which men would fill. That is the first myth.
The second, and perhaps the more pernicious, is the idea that women work simply for luxuries. Again, if I may refer to figures for January 28 of this year, there were 4,015,000 women in the labour force of whom 391,000 were either divorced, widowed or separated, supporting themselves or their dependents. Another 1,167,000 were single women supporting themselves. These people were clearly not looking upon work as a luxury but as a necessity, and the right to enjoy equal access to jobs is of fundamental importance to them. Again, in relation to married women who are working, according to an economist for the Advisory Council on the Status of Women, almost 45 per cent of the married women in the labour force belong to families which, but for their earnings, would be living well below the poverty line. It is these people who suffer most by the continual refusal of the government to accept its responsibilities and get the Canadian economy moving again.
I do not want to suggest that the problem is simply one the solution of which is at the feet of this government. I think there is no sector of society hat can be proud of its record in recognizing the modern reau.y that women in this country deserve the right to work as equals with men. If we look at industry, the statistics show that discrimination continues very severely in many industries in the country. In 1976, Labour Canada statistics show that of people in management and administrative categories in the country only 18.6 per cent are women. Similarly of Canadians working in engineering, research and mathematics, categories that can be seen as being executive or senior positions, only 9.6 per cent are women. We have no absolute data on the private sector but we have some startling statistics which have to do with government incursions, particularly the incursions of the Government of Canada into the private sector relating to Crown corporations.
It might be useful to the House, since the minister who is so proud of the record of his government is here, to review the role of women in senior management in some of the Crown corporations in this country. In Canadian National Railways, in senior management positions there are 1,014 men and 2 women; in Air Canada, in senior management positions there are 158 men and 1 woman; in the Bank of Canada in senior management positions there are 17 men and 1 woman; in the National Harbours Board in senior positions there are 55 men
March 6, 1978

and 3 women. That is an indication of the degree of commitment of this government to ensure that emanations of the Government of Canada reflect in reality equality for the women of Canada.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-EQUALITY OF RIGHTS FOR WOMEN IN LABOUR FORCE
speechtext: Shame!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-EQUALITY OF RIGHTS FOR WOMEN IN LABOUR FORCE
speechtext: How many women do you have in parliament?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-EQUALITY OF RIGHTS FOR WOMEN IN LABOUR FORCE
speechtext: We will have a great many more from the Dollard constituency.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-EQUALITY OF RIGHTS FOR WOMEN IN LABOUR FORCE
speechtext: I invite you personally.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-EQUALITY OF RIGHTS FOR WOMEN IN LABOUR FORCE
speechtext:
I am very pleased the Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. Goyer) has returned from Africa. I am sure that if an issue arises relating to his department regarding which questions might be placed to him, he will get out of the country again.
In relation to organized labour and to labour unions, I think it is appropriate for the minister to pay tribute to some of the women leaders in union movements in the country who have played a prominent role. But it is also important for us to recognize that labour unions have not been active enough in trying to organize among Canadians in lower income groups where working women tend to predominate. That is a record of which the unions of the country cannot be proud, just as industries in the country cannot be proud of their record in terms of ensuring that there is an adequate role and a more nearly equal role for women in the direction of Canadian industry.
Certainly in relation to the Public Service of Canada 1 will say, without getting into this matter at any length at this time, that the statistics speak for themselves. To the end of December 31, 1977, there were 95,922 women in the public service, only 33.9 per cent of the total public service labour force. What is even more striking than that is what those people earn. Of that, nearly 100,000 women in the public service only 299 earn more than $30,000 a year. That indicates again that we have not made nearly enough progress in industry, in unions, and in the government in trying to ensure a more nearly equal opportunity for the women of this country.
Naturally we intend to support the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby. It is a motion which deserves support and I hope it will receive it from all corners of the House. But I think that the danger with that motion, its weakness and limitation, are that it is not sufficiently specific, and I can understand the reason for it. Later on I will be submitting an amendment which 1 hope will add some specific proposals on which the Government and the Parliament of Canada may act immediately. Certainly, with regard to the general nature of that motion, it is important that we recognize in the country how badly served Canadian women are by the current economic situation.
The most recent figures available to us indicate-I am quoting now from the document called "Women in the Labour Force":
Status of Women
The average annual earnings of men employees who worked 50 to 52 weeks, increased $4,183 from 1969 to 1974 compared with $2,369 for women.
There is obviously a case of a double standard there. In the same publication we read:
The average annual earnings of women employees who worked 40 to 49 weeks were 34,293 in 1974, compared with $8,463 for men. The earnings of men exceeded those of women by 97.1 per cent.
The publication goes on to state:
Averaged across the country, average hourly industrial wage rates for men exceeded those of women in all similarly described occupations for which data were available in 1975.
Those are not new statistics. That is precisely the problem. That situation has been in existence for far too long, and this is the government which has mounted a campaign of public relations in place of action. It should have accepted its obligation to change those statistics which continue to condemn women to a secondary position in the life of Canada.
As I said, the motion of my friend, the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby, is clearly accurate in its generality, but it is important that we specify some of the individual reforms on which we can act now and on which the government can act now, given its control of the agenda, and could introduce quickly in the House, if it actually wanted to give priority to these matters.
We have to bear in mind that even though the problems of women are aggravated by the serious economic problems of this country, even in good times there will continue to be a double standard which is discriminatory against women in this country, unless the government in Ottawa is prepared to accept more reforms, to be bolder and to honor its commitments and act, instead of talking, in direct contrast to the way this government has proceeded.
There are some reforms that are directly within the control of the government. One of them relates to the discriminatory practices of federal government agencies. Clearly one of them is the Unemployment Insurance Commission. In the comprehensive review of the unemployment insurance program in Canada women are referred to as "secondary income earners with unstable employment patterns", thus leaving the reader that strong impression that their salaries are not an essential part of the family income. The Advisory Council on the Status of Women indicates that it has received a number of complaints from women who have been discriminated against when applying for and receiving unemployment insurance benefits. One could go on at some length quoting from that record, but the fact is that we need to eliminate those discriminatory practices. We need new training and job placement assistance for unemployed women in Canada, and that should be acted upon by this government as a priority.
We have seriously discriminatory laws which could be changed with little trouble in this country. Colleagues of mine will be speaking at greater length later. One of the problems has to do with the tax situation of unincorporated small businesses and farms. It is not permitted now to extend salaries to working wives. My colleague, the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald) will, I am sure, elaborate

March 6, 1978
Status of Women
on the problem that this causes for Canadian women. A second discriminatory law, which will be again a matter raised by the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands, has to do with the pension situation in this country. There are a number of matters that have to be changed there, but we want to give parliament an opportunity to address itself to the most unfair single instance of discrimination in the matter of pensions, that is, the instance of female spouses who receive spouse's allowance because their husbands are eligible by age for pensions. In this country, with a government which claims to care about women, that allowance is cut off when the spouse who receives the pension dies. This means that in the case of too many women across the country we have a situation where they are left without a spouse and without a pension at the same time. Clearly that must be changed, and any government which was prepared to honour its commitment truly to women would be acting on that change immediately and would receive quick support from this side of the House.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-EQUALITY OF RIGHTS FOR WOMEN IN LABOUR FORCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-EQUALITY OF RIGHTS FOR WOMEN IN LABOUR FORCE
speechtext:
Within the direct responsibility of the government there are a number of programs where the government, instead of repeating old speeches, can set an example of equality. I think of the career assignment program. I understand that even though this program is designed to develop the individual for advancement into senior levels of the civil service, at present the maximum quota for women is 10 per cent. That is a clear discrimination established by the government itself.
Again, there should be changes in the approach to the administrative trainee program. In 1976 less than one per cent of those people eligible to participate in this program actually participated. This is a statistic from the annual report of the Public Service Commission. The reason given for this is that the very low participation by women can be accounted for by the fact that the program is not at all widely promoted, and people at that level are support people who are considered to be too valuable in their present capacities to be allowed the time to improve their qualifications.
With all that in mind, and those changes that can be introduced on behalf of and in the interests of the women in Canada, in approving of the general direction of the motion introduced by my colleague, the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby, I should like to move, seconded by the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands:
That the motion be amended by adding thereto the following words: and consequently directs the government immediately to act to end such discrimination and ensure equality for women particularly by developing policies:
(1)	to eliminate discriminatory manpower and unemployment insurance commission practices and implement new training and job placement assistance for unemployed women;
(2)	to encourage women's participation in unincorporated family farms and businesses by allowing the deduction of salaries paid to spouses;
(3)	to ensure that women are not deprived of spouse's security pension benefits upon their husband's death; and,

(4)	to accelerate the promotion of women to an equitable share of senior public service positions by guaranteeing their access to executive training such as the Career Advancement Program.
In his remarks the minister admitted that not everything has been done. What we have done in this amendment is spell out four areas in which the government could act immediately. This amendment gives the Government of Canada an opportunity to take action today on a real agenda of reformation for the women of Canada. It is a place to start in making this a country of equal opportunity for Canadian women. I hope the minister and the government will remember the reality of their claim of interest in the women of Canada by supporting these specific recommendations for action on behalf of women, action that can be taken now if the Government of Canada chooses to do so.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-EQUALITY OF RIGHTS FOR WOMEN IN LABOUR FORCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first I would want to commend the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby (Mr. Broadbent) for putting to the House this motion that women ought to have the same rights as men, on a social level as well as in all economic sectors, and we want to condemn the present government, as well as all its predecessors, for its discriminatory policies regarding Canadian women.
This is not the first time we ask the government to table legislation which will free women from past myths and allow them to live freely in all spheres of this century of change. Quoting numerous pieces of legislation passed by the House, I stated that almost 75 per cent of our so-called social legislation is in fact anti-social legislation, from the oldest and most archaic to the most recent. The government tables an impeccable bill, which at first sight we would tend to approve, but further study reveals that it is only eyewash, although many hon. members fall for it.
The laws governing our economy were written for one purpose only, that of protecting the strong while crushing the weak; and when the weak are too poor, too much in debt, then the government acts the good Samaritan and comes to their help with a pittance to keep them from starving to death. That is the very basis of our beautiful capitalistic economy. Let us add to that the conviction that our society is made up of the stronger sex and the weaker one, and the picture is complete. Speaking of the weaker sex, Mr. Speaker, by which term we still designate today's woman, the newspapers told us the best one yet a few weeks ago by relaying some statistics. In Canada, country of traditions, the large majority of husbands
March 6, 1978

still beat their wives, while in the United States we have proof that more wives beat their husbands than vice versa. We can therefore say the United States beat us to the punch on that one. Will we see the day when women will become the stronger sex? Everything is possible with modern techniques!
In revising our few statutes on women, we are surprised to discover that some of them seem unalterable. Since I have been sitting in this House, and especially during the six election campaigns in which I have taken part, how many people have I heard plead the case against the secular discrimination which has been the lot of women? Men as well as women MP's have begged parliament to do justice to the women who work and the women who have chidren. And we will hear more of them even today but will that change anything? Not much if we go by past interventions. We had the Year of the Woman and no law of substance was passed; that is to say that we still hang on to the traditional laws that go back to Canada's beginnings, or were even transmitted directly to us from their countries of origin where women had no legal rights though they participated personally and to a large extent in the economy of the country.
Perhaps some will say that I am exaggerating and that today's woman is a first class member of our society. Let us rather consider the case of a legally wedded couple and let us suppose that both spouses are working outside and that they decide to buy a house. Do you know that legally speaking the husband alone can sign the contract? If the representative of the law invites the wife to sign it is merely a gesture of courtesy on his part for her signature has only a symbolic value. The true owner of the building is the husband even if his wife pays for two-thirds of it. Yet no one among our great legal wizards who are ruling us has the courage to rid our society of this backward tradition which is so humiliating for working women.
The same system applies to the rights regarding children. Although it is the mother who bears the child and gives him birth it is the father who exercises the basic rights. However, only the mother can confirm who is the father of a child for in our funny society, one has to realize that if the husband can fool his wife the opposite may also be true. So there is a risk of granting to the man rights which he never had on the child in the first place.
When the supporter of this motion blames the government for its discriminatory wage policy toward women in the labour force I concede that perhaps the government should have acted more rapidly. However one must not forget that it is the industrial sector which opened its doors to women first, and given the fact that after the thirties the big industries were the masters in the field of employment, since the unions had not yet started to organize the workers, you can conclude that it was not for humanitarian considerations that these same com-
Status of Women
panies called on women workers but rather to get cheap labour.
In spite of tremendous hardships and obstacles, women, as well as men, have slowly organized to improve their working conditions. Some will ask why the governments of the time did not react. It was just impossible. Just as it is not yet possible today for the good reason that no one can serve two masters at a time. The governments have always been dependent on financiers. This is the main reason, although unavowed, why the government can not act directly to end discrimination against female workers in Canada.
We have always advocated equal pay for equal work. We will continue to say that a woman deserves equal retribution in relation with her work in any area of the economy. As so well stated the other day by the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Lambert), we will continue to fight to obtain an income for the mother at home.
Mr. Speaker, we consider that if there is an an individual who takes part in the Canadian economy it is the mother who devotes every minute of her time to her home to protect the necessary human assets for the survival of Canada. As for myself, I feel that the part of the mother working at home to educate her children and take care of them is much superior to that of a social or industrial worker. This is why they deserve more from this country. In fact, we are dealing with discrimination against women in Canada, but the worst kind of discrimination involving the greatest number of women in Canada is the one faced by homemakers. For the most part they accepted their role of their free will and accord. They are accused of having chosen the ghetto. But shopwork would have condemned them to feeding machines, a 100 times more enslaving type of occupation. At least, they have no bosses, they are self-employed. And they perform the most marvelous, the most needed type of function in the country, to which that of senior bureaucrats is no match. In that respect, Mr. Speaker, I had the sad surprise of reading in Hansard for February 27, 1978 the statements by the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mrs. Holt). She could not sit here and listen to this kind of tokenism, perpetuation of role locking a woman into the role of homemaker a place in life she may not choose. Utterly ridiculous, indeed utterly false. She even added, for the benefit of husbands, if you want to pay your wife, pay her yourself; the country should not have to pay the cost. As if the freely and consciously married woman were her husband's slave. I object to that suggestion.
Mr. Speaker, how could the husband pay his wife when he gets the same salary as a bachelor, and still he has one or two or three children to support on top of that? The hon. member no doubt will say, as did the minister this afternoon, that the husband has an income tax deduction for his wife and children. Do you believe a deduction will pay for the clothes and apparel needed by his wife? Family allowances will not even pay for children's food, let alone clothes and the cost of

March 6, 1978
Status of Women
education. Who would suggest this could balance the family budget? It is financially impossible. This financial aspect is responsible for the worst kind of discrimination at home, and the homemaker is the first victim because she will not be able to afford help for well deserved holidays. She will even have to do without things needed in order to ensure her children's future. This prompts us to urge homemakers' salaries.
As I said, I object to the comments by the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway. First, because outside work does not necessarily free women, and second, because homemakers, just like their husbands are committed to the care of their children the human stock needed by every country. Unless the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway feels human stock is less important than the stock of money, I cannot find an explanation to her reaction to the motion put forward by the hon. member for Bellechasse.
I see no discrimination in the fact that a mother would choose to stay home to take care of her children, since this would not be for her a ghetto, but a liberation, and a freely chosen liberation. Moreover, I do not believe that a mother who takes care exclusively of her family has been forced into it. This is not true! If the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway were to communicate with several of the charwomen who work at night in the Parliament buildings, perhaps she would change her mind because I contacted them myself and I know that 75 per cent of them would be very happy to stay home if they had a guaranteed income.
In reading the speech of the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway, I wondered if she had ever met happy families, and I mean by this a man, a woman and children. There still are households where there is no discrimination, where the father and mother are partners who live in harmony with the children because there is a dialogue based on mutual trust. We do not hear about those families, perhaps because, as the song says, happy people have no story while the unfortunate proclaim their misfortune. This is why they seem to outnumber happy people. If the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway came to my constituency, I could show her families with two, three, four and even five children who would tell her: We are happy. We are not millionnaires, but we have love and basic security. Of course, it is always necessary to improve the financial situation, but the social situation is healthy and this is the most important. Of course, the husband works hard in the fields, in the plant or thousands of feet under ground in the mines for 20 or 25 years, and I can assure you that he has no time for outside amusement like the hon. member suggests.
During all those years, the housewife has a marvellous role to play and she participates voluntarily in our Canadian economy. To this woman, I would say: You deserve more credit than all social workers, all women at work in industry, all secretaries and even many members of Parliament. If we honour the soldier who gives his life for his country, how should we reward the housewife who gives several lives to her

country? When we speak about discrimination, we should be very careful, because we can often provoke it unknowningly, just like we are most often the cause of our own misfortune, because we often want too much when happiness is quite near. We must never forget that happiness is a state of mind in that those who look for it exclusively elsewhere expose themselves to terrible deceptions.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons

speechtext: Order, please. I will recognize the hon. member for York South (Mrs. Appolloni) in a moment. I have examined the amendment moved by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark). Instead of waiting until eight o'clock to announce a decision, I will make my ruling now. I feel that the amendment does not add any matter which is foreign to the basic proposal contained in the motion of the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby (Mr. Broadbent). I admit that the amendment does single out specific alternatives, but it would achieve the same objective. I think it just adds to the first proposal. I am therefore putting now to the House the amendment proposed earlier by the hon. Leader of the Opposition.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-EQUALITY OF RIGHTS FOR WOMEN IN LABOUR FORCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am usually careful not to attribute motives to speakers, but I really wonder what we are all doing here today. I once said to a reporter that I felt we in Ottawa were living in a fishbowl. If that is true, I think today's fishbowl is full of red herrings.
The mover of this motion, the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby (Mr. Broadbent), has been around this House for ten years. According to Hansard, in those ten years he has spent a grand total of 29 minutes speaking about the status of women. The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) has been in this parliament seven years, and he has spent the grand total of five minutes speaking about the status of women. At first a woman might think it is great that some people are really interested in our status, in our predicament and in our well being, and she might wonder what will come of all this, but the speakers who have given us their gems of wisdom so far have been highly selective with the statistics they have been using.
They have been even more selective with the types of women they would like to help. Members of the NDP discuss only working women. The motion before us today states the following:
That this House asserts that the women of Canada ought to have fully equal rights in participating in the Canadian economy . ..
What a statement! Is that to say that up until now the women of Canada have had no participation in the Canadian economy? Shame! If it had not been for the women of Canada we would not have an economy at all, and hon. members should get that into their heads. The motion presumes that women have had nothing to do with the economy and have been so downtrodden that they have not done anything. The hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby forgets that the chairman of the Economic Council of Canada is a woman. Who appointed her? It was not the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby-he
March 6, 1978

could not do that-but this government, which is now being soundly chastised for not having done its job with regard to women.
Is it not interesting that the member now speaking also happens to be a woman? I was not elected because I was a woman. I did not want that. I was elected because the people of York South thought I would be a good representative.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-EQUALITY OF RIGHTS FOR WOMEN IN LABOUR FORCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-EQUALITY OF RIGHTS FOR WOMEN IN LABOUR FORCE
speechtext:
I said I would try to overlook motives, even though there is something asking me whether this is really real or something phony like a $3 bill.
On December 14 we were discussing the Canada Labour Code in this House. As vice-chairman of the committee discussing the Canada Labour Code, Bill C-8-and I have been around all the time-I can say that one particular clause recognizes not only the importance of women but also the needs of women. One of those needs is maternity leave. One would think that the opposition parties, which are so concerned about us poor things, would welcome maternity leave. Not on your sweet life! On December 14 the hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Ritchie) said the following:
Turning to the Canada Labour Code, I would like to point out that section 59(4) of the code currently prohibits the dismissal of pregnant employees ...
Let me just stop there. In an effort to give us equal status hon. members have to find words other than "women". Let me point out that only women can be pregnant. In order to avoir being called sexist or something, he calls us "pregnant employees". Good for him. He went on:
... prohibits the dismissal of pregnant employees only if they have compiled twelve consecutive months of continuous employment. That condition-
The condition of employment, not of pregnancy.
-is now to be removed altogether, but I suggest the problem with regard to pregnancy is not solved that easily ...
The hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Ritchie) obviously knows that pregnancy is a very serious problem and it is not easy to solve. He continued:
I suppose legislators feel that being pregnant should not be a job disqualification under any circumstances.
I am trying hard not to laugh, Mr. Speaker.
However, with certain people pregnancy is almost incapacitating. As long as pregnant employees can do their usual work, no one complains;-
Isn't that nice!
-but in certain circumstances pregnant employees are often just 'around' and are not in a physical condition to contribute their usual work output. In some instances, this amounts to wages without any work being performed. The matter of pregnancy should be studied further.
I agree.
Pregnancy cannot be treated as a nonevent, and a pregnant person-
We are getting better, Mr. Speaker; now it is a "pregnant person".
-should not automatically receive the usual work benefits.
Status of Women
Mr. Speaker, is this the kind of view that would come from a person who is genuinely interested in the status of women? He could not even bring himself to say it is a woman who has a baby. If he does not understand the fundamental point it is rather superfluous to continue from there. I am not saying that his thinking is typical of the Tory party, heaven forbid! I could not bring myself to say that. 1 might think it on several occasions but I will never say it. This is the kind of thing that the women of Canada are faced with.
Hon. members opposite cannot even talk properly. This afternoon the Leader of the Opposition was trying not to laugh. Frankly, I think he was trying not to gag and it was his nervousness that made him seem as if he were trying not to laugh. Why are people so hung up? I can tell you why, Mr. Speaker, and this is what is at the bottom of the problems of women in Canada and in the world. People use rhetoric and phrases like "equal rights", "equal pay". The hon. member for Roberval (Mr. Gauthier) said "equal pay for equal work." If that is what he is looking for I think we are going to be in trouble not for the next ten years but for the next ten centuries.
What I want for the women of Canada is equality of status-to know that we are exactly the same, that we have the same dignity whether we choose to work outside the home or inside the home. If people are going to get hung up on big rhetorical sentences like "equal pay" and "equal job opportunities," that will be absolutely devastating to the women of Canada. Those who prefer to stay at home and mind their children-and God bless them, they are the foundation of our society-would get a complex. Must they go out and produce for the gross national product? That is a kind of thing they are being pushed into and they resent it. We must stop these pious utterances and get down to an understanding of where we are. If hon. members do not have that understanding they should have the humility to ask.
I listened to the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby and thought that as a socialist he sounded terribly snobbish. He graded jobs and spoke of those that could be rejected by men. The jobs he rejected, the ones that he gave the impression he thought were a little bit below human dignity, were clerical jobs and sales jobs. What is the matter with any job at all as long as it is done by a person who enjoys doing it? The person who does the secretarial job or any other kind should never be told that he or she is inferior by reason of the job. That has nothing to do with human dignity. To tell a person that she or he is "down" is a self-fulfilling prophecy. If they want to move from jobs they should be encouraged.
How can this be done? Let us consider the work force again, and ask why most women have problems entering it. One reason is lack of education, and that it can be formal education. But more than, that it is attitude. The hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby spoke of his children, a boy of 18, and a girl of five. The girl is only five, Mr. Speaker, but he was worried about whether she would get a good job. If my child were still five I would be worried about whether she would be a happy human being. That is all there is to it. Does she want a job, or

March 6, 1978
Status of Women
does she want to stay home? If she decides to stay home, will she be given the same dignity as if she had a Ph.D. in sociology or something else? Will she be given opportunities not because she is a girl but because she is a person? That is what we want in this country-equality of status; we want all to be treated the same, whether male or female. I do not know if that is happening, Mr. Speaker.
I hope I heard the hon. member for Roberval correctly-or maybe it would be better if I had not heard him correctly. I think he told us that in Canada we have a very large percentage of battered wives. That is true and it is a terrible tragedy for society. Then he said things were better in the United States because they had battered husbands and maybe one day we would catch up to them. I want to tell the hon. member that if he thinks that getting equality of status for women means that Canadian women can batter their husbands, he should forget it. We do not want that kind of equality.

speechtext:
I suggest he add that to the record, Mr. Speaker-joke, joke, joke. I was not amused but that is another point.
I hope that when speaking in this debate hon. members will try not to patronize; there is nothing we want less than a patronizing attitude, attitudes such as "Sure we will help you, little DP", as I have sometimes been called. We do not want a pat on the rear or any other part of the anatomy. We want help when we ask for it, and constructive help, not the patronizing help that we have had for so long, though not from this government.
Now I come back to motives, Mr. Speaker. I think the real cause of our problems is attitudes. We all know that attitudes cannot be legislated but they can be influenced by legislation. I have to say that this government does just that. Bill C-8 is a classic example of what the government is trying to do. Apart from the maternity leave clause, there is nothing in the bill that puts women lower than their male counterparts, and for that I am grateful.
The Leader of the Opposition said that his party is concerned about UIC. Maybe he did not know he was talking to a person who was chairman of the board of referees of the UIC. As hon. members can see, I happen to be female. But I did not get that job because I was female, I got it because I was a damned good chairman. That is what we should have all the

time. Do not put us in just because we are female. You are not doing any good to any person by setting up society, Mr. Speaker. Put us in because you take the trouble to listen to what we are saying, and then act upon it.
I remember that in 1974, like every other candidate, I had to sign my nomination form in the returning officer's office. One part of the form asked for my occupation. I could have said I was a musician, which is true. I could have said I am a writer, which is also true. I could have said I am a social worker, which is also true. But I did not say I was any of those. I put down the occupation which has given me the most satisfaction in my life, that is, the rearing of my children. I could not say "child rearer" because they would have thought I was peculiar, so I put down "housewife". Mr. Speaker, you have no idea of the kind of reaction I have had to that since and during my campaign-"You, a housewife!"
I must say that this attitude, this negativeness, did not come only from men. I remember I was canvassing in one particularly rich, affluent part of my riding which contained beautiful big houses. I knocked at the door and this beautifully coiffured woman came to the door. Her nails were manicured. It had been raining that day and I had been canvassing. I probably looked like a drowned dog. I said: "Hi, I am your candidate". Behind her I could see a woman who was scrubbing the floors very hard. This woman at the door said: "I cannot vote for you, you are only a housewife, just like me".
I was not like her at all because I had no one at home scrubbing my floors and I did not have time to have my hair done or my nails manicured. The whole point was her attitude of putting me down. I could have argued and said that I am this and that, which was all true, but I decided that as a matter of privilege and principle I would not do that. I may have lost her vote, but quite frankly I do not think I was going to get it in the first place. This is the kind of attitude that we must get rid of. It is the kind of attitude that women face in the labour force everywhere. A woman applies for a job and first of all she is looked up and down. They wonder when she will become pregnant or if she will become pregnant. Whether a woman is married or not has nothing to do with that; we have got beyond that stage, thank heaven. That is the first thought, the biological one.
Then they wonder if the woman will become emotional in any given situation. Since when have women had the monopoly on emotion? This is the kind of stereotype which we have been prone to all our lives. Things are getting better, they are improving. Let us keep it like that.
I would ask members of the opposition, indeed members of all three parties, if they are sincere in their efforts, to do something concrete. But please do not give women any more platitudes. Do not patronize them. If hon. members want to find the real culprit, make sure they point the finger at the right person. It is not the government of Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, March 8, this Wednesday, has been declared International Women's Day by the United Nations. Whether it is appropriate or not that in this day and age a day must be set aside for the recognition of the rights of half the world's population is debatable in itself, but surely it is less than appropriate, in fact downright degrading, that in the Canadian House of Commons in 1978 it should be necessary to discuss the discrimination and inequities against women in the labour force. We should long ago have arrived at the point where equality of women in the work force is a matter of fact and not a matter of debate. That this issue must still be debated, that the necessity for it exists, is a sad reflection on Canadian society.
The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) this afternoon clearly stated where the Progressive Conservative party stands and the concerns that we have on the motion presented in the House today. However, I would like to pay tribute to one of the continuing advocates of women's rights in this House, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles).

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-EQUALITY OF RIGHTS FOR WOMEN IN LABOUR FORCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-EQUALITY OF RIGHTS FOR WOMEN IN LABOUR FORCE
speechtext:
Consistently over the years he has spoken out on behalf of women, especially with regard to their woefully inadequate pension situation. I, along with thousands of Canadians, was appalled at the recent unkind and unnecessary reference by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) to the hon. member as a left-over from the depression days. I cannot emphasize enough that the country and certainly the government can do with much more of the concern and compassion shown by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. That concern and compassion are rooted in his memories of the depression and the setback and resulting inequities that that depression caused the women in the labour force. The Prime Minister and his colleagues, who cannot or will not remember those injustices, seem only too willing to let them happen again
Status of Women
now at a time when our economy is once more being hit by high prices and high unemployment.
In 1975 the United Nations General Assembly adopted the World Plan of Action as a guideline for the international decade for women, 1976-1985. The minister seemed to have heard about it for the first time this afternoon. Well, Canada supported that program. It supported the plan of action. One of the steps recommended at that time was set out in these terms:
Governments should formulate policies and action programs, directed toward equality of opportunity and treatment for women workers, to guarantee their right to equal pay.
Further, to ensure that declaration, it recommended:
Special efforts are needed to foster positive attitudes among employers, workers, men and women in society and to eliminate obstacles based on sex-typed divisions of labour.
When it comes to special efforts to foster positive attitudes, as the United Nations agreement recommended, this government's lack of concern and inaction are laid bare, because any special efforts that the government has undertaken in recent months seem to have been designed to foster negative, not positive, attitudes.
Why do I say that? At times of high unemployment, there is, unfortunately, tragically still a backlash against women in the work force. It has happened before and it is happening again now. Anyone who is aware of the social development and the changes of the twenties and thirties will be quick to see the comparison with today. In the twenties, women made great inroads into the labour force, but the lack of jobs in the thirties created social pressures on them and the result was that many women left the labour market.
Again in the sixties and seventies we saw women making inroads into the job market. But now at a time of high unemployment the old, socially ingrained assumptions about the status of women, assumptions which are being fostered by the government, are reappearing and serve to build up a guilt complex about whether women have the right to be full members of the labour force. Did the government fulfil its commitment to foster positive attitudes? No. Instead, the government has led the way in subtly applying pressure on women by equating the high unemployment figures with the increased participation of women in the work force.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) did this directly. In his speech in Toronto on January 16, he said:
In the next year, unemployment will again depend to a considerable extent on the participation rate, especially among women and young people.
Then on February 16, the minister responsible for the status of women pointed to the rise in the participation of both women and youth in the labour force and said:
This suggests a degree of competition for jobs between youth and women over 25, a hypothesis which tends to be supported by the fact that employment of young people and adult women is concentrated in similar industrial sectors.
On the surface these statements may not appear to be terribly damnable. Evidently the government does not think so.

March 6, 1978
Status of Women
The minister responsible for the status of women says such statements simply reflect reality. In response to a question I put to him on this matter, he replied:
I rejoice, as does this government, in the fact that women are joining the work force in greater numbers but obviously one should not ignore this phenomenon in terms of its impact on unemployment.
In my view, these statements, which are so characteristic of the government, are damnable and they are doubly so. First, they encourage negative attitudes about women in the work force, creating social pressures on women to get out of the labour market and inciting fear in others that their jobs might be threatened.
In the second place, those statements are not true. They are myths masquerading as excuses for the government's lack of solutions to the country's economic ills. They are not borne out by the facts. Women are not taking jobs from men. Regrettable though it is, there is still job segregation in this country. Women are still filling, for the most part, clerical and service positions. They are stenographers, typists or receptionists, cooks, waitresses, hairdressers, teachers. Three quarters of all working women are employed in only five occupational categories-clerical, services, sales, nursing and teaching. The labour force is "ghettoized". Women hold the jobs that men have traditionally turned away from. Not only that, but the jobs in which the women in the work force are slotted are the lower paid ones. Women are locked into a system which pays them less when they work and less when they retire.
When I questioned the basis of that ministerial statement linking high unemployment to the participation of women in the work force, I did so with good reason. In what sectors are the highest pockets of male unemployment to be found? One immediately thinks of construction, forestry and logging, mining, fishing and trapping. We saw recently that 3,000 miners were laid off in Sudbury and Thompson. It was not women marching into the mines that put those men out of work. Adult women are not competing with young engineers or young graduates, or young welders and woodworkers. If there is, in fact, any competition going on for jobs between women and men, it is that because of the bad employment situation men are moving into areas which have traditionally been filled by women. This would be laudable if it reflected a change in attitude, if it really did mean desegregation of the job market rather than a mere reflection of the shortage of jobs. The Federation of Women Teachers' Associations of Ontario tells us that the traditional female occupation of elementary teaching has seen an increase of 10 per cent in the number of men and a drop of 5 per cent in the number of women in the past five years. Now I ask: Who is taking jobs from whom in this situation?
A second myth, one which goes hand in hand with the first, is that women are second wage earners and that their jobs are a luxury. This is simply not true. Over a million and a half are working women who are either single, widowed, separated or divorced. They do not have a husband's salary to fall back on. Many of these are single parents with just as many financial commitments as their male colleagues, perhaps more.

The worst myth of all, and the one that lurks behind the other two, is that women who work in the home and who are dependent on their husband's incomes are automatically taken care of for life. None of the myths about women fly so directly into the face of reality as does this one.
Let me tell the House something about these women, the ones who worked at home for husband, family and community and who are now widowed or divorced. Some of them are in the position in which they find themselves today because they gave in to the social pressures of the thirties and left the work force. The recent report of the Canadian Council on Social Development states, with regard to women and pensions, that the rate of poverty among the female elderly is shocking. Using the poverty line established by the Senate Committee on Poverty, $3,988 for a single person based on 1975 data, we find that almost two thirds of women aged between 65 and 70 and three-quarters of women aged 70 and over are poor; they do not receive an income of $3,988.
That is the situation of women over 65. The plight of women between 60 and 65 who are widowed, divorced or single is simply appalling. They are not entitled to the old age pension or to the guaranteed income supplement. They are not supported by a husband and they are often unable to get work because of their age. After years of faithful service to their homes and society, these women are at the mercy of the welfare rolls.
Let me read just one letter from one of these women, a widow who can no longer work and who lives on $1,850 a year. This woman was left a widow in 1953. She had three young children to look after. She writes:
I went back to school . .. and looking after my children was all I could manage. My parents looked after my 3 while I was away at school for the few hours ... when my oldest daughter turned 14 she went to work at Xmas, Easter and summer holidays. The same with the younger two. They all had no holidays including me. We all had to work to make ends meet.
Now, ill and elderly, her reward for her hard labour both at home and in the work force is a life of poverty.
Anyone who has been similarly following the reports of the hearings of the Ontario Royal Commission on the Status of Pensions will be only too familiar with the plight of the elderly, many of whom are as badly off as the one example of the 63-year old Toronto woman who is an unemployed stenographer. She is too young for the basic old age pension and says she lives on rhubarb and rice in the summer and onions and rice in the winter. This woman has worked steadily for 30 years and feels, quite rightly, that she is entitled to her pension now. "If they wait much longer", she says, "I'll be dead before I can collect it."
The situation about which I have been speaking is one in which women are losers whichever way they turn. If they work only in the home during their lifetime, our present pension laws do not favour them. In fact, it discriminates against them and, unless a benevolent husband has seen to their needs, they are not adequately provided for in old age.
March 6, 1978

Even the women who work outside the home get the short end of the pension stick. The Toronto woman to whom I just referred had been in the labour force for some 30 years, probably without any pension benefits. Whether or not private or public pension schemes actually discriminate against women, the fact remains that since women are disqualified from full and equal participation in the work force they are disadvantaged from the outset with regard to pensions. Their low paying jobs, their requirement to move in and out of the work force to care for children, the obstacles in their way to make it to the top of the career ladder; all of these factors work against women who seek financial independence both in their work and in their retirement. The deck is stacked against them.
Surely this government can and should be helping women to get out of this rut of dependence, this frustration of dependency. First of all, quite contrary to what the minister was talking about this afternoon, it can foster positive attitudes towards women in the work force by ceasing to equate the influx of women into the work force with the high unemployment rate. This is essential to women taking their rightful place in the economic life of the country and would work toward allowing them to better prepare themselves for their retirement, just as men are able to do.
Secondly, the government should allow women who choose to work at home to contribute to the Canada Pension Plan and to have pensions in their own right. Until the work of women in the home is recognized as a legitimate contribution to society and their need for retirement pay recognized equally with that of men, elderly women will continue to live in poverty.
I have spoken before in the House on this-

Thank you, sir, and I thank the House for that courtesy.
I have spoken in the House before on this subject of housewives and pensions. I have heard the arguments of the government against such an amendment to the Canada Pension Plan, and while there may be difficulties in implementing voluntary contributions for housewives, I suggest that the difficulties can be overcome if there is a will to do so. Both Germany and France have been able to accommodate voluntary contributions from housewives in their national pension schemes. Can we in Canada not find a way as well?
Finally, Mr. Speaker, the government can act now to alleviate the plight of single, divorced and widowed women in the 60 to 65 age bracket. So many of these women are living on less than $2,000 a year, most of it from welfare. The first step in this direction, and one that would cost the federal treasury less than $400,000 a year, would be to cease the Scrooge-like
Status of Women
practice of withdrawing the spouse's allowance upon the death of one marriage partner.
What kind of a double standard do we have on the part of the government when it comes to making expenditures of its funds? We saw only last week that it allows a payment of some $2 million in fees to a sales agent for nuclear reactors without any work having been done, or any expected, and there is no effort to be made to retrieve that money, yet at the same time the government peremptorily cuts off the payment of less than half a million dollars in total to some 2,500 spouses who have worked hard all their lives in the interests of this country.
This heartless practice which causes tremendous hardship among those who least deserve it, and which represents such a paltry saving to the national budget, should be discontinued immediately. The surviving spouse should be allowed to keep her spouse's allowance.
I emphasize that this is just a preliminary step toward easing the financial burden of this particular group of people. It covers only widows and does not cover separated, divorced or single women living on inadequate incomes. It creates inequities, but it is a step in the right direction and would indicate a more positive attitude toward the needs and the rights of elderly women who have worked long and hard in the home.
If the present discrimination against women in the work force is allowed to continue, then we will still be dealing with these problems of pension discrimination in 50 years' time. Our society will be judged by how it eliminates discriminatory practices. 1 say to you, sir, that if that judgment were to be rendered now it would not be a favourable one.
