Mr. Speaker, as the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald) has pointed out, it is a sad commentary on our times that it is necessary to put down a motion in the House of Commons calling for recognition of equal rights for the women of Canada; yet the fact is that such a motion is necessary, and in my view the House should support the motion tonight in the name of the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby (Mr. Broadbent).
We also welcome the amendment moved by the Official Opposition. We shall be voting for it when the time comes, and we hope the House as a whole will recognize the validity of the amendment as well as of the motion.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-EQUALITY OF RIGHTS FOR WOMEN IN LABOUR FORCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-EQUALITY OF RIGHTS FOR WOMEN IN LABOUR FORCE
speechtext:
The two speakers from the government side who took part in the debate this afternoon but are not here tonight tried to make something of the allegation that the interest in the well-being of women from this side of the House was something new. I noticed that the charge was not levelled in my direction. It so happens that during the first year I was in this House, which is now more than 35 years ago, I raised questions about the pensions or non-pensions of widows of veterans of the first world war. I

March 6, 1978
Status of Women
raised questions as to the inadequate pensions of the widows of civil servants; and I raised matters having to do with the low pay of the women doing the menial work in this building. In other words, I have been at this for a long time.
I also recall, and I checked the record this afternoon to make sure of it, that it was in 1950, 28 years ago, that I started the campaign for the establishment of a women's bureau within the Department of Labour. It was a five year battle.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-EQUALITY OF RIGHTS FOR WOMEN IN LABOUR FORCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-EQUALITY OF RIGHTS FOR WOMEN IN LABOUR FORCE
speechtext:
I was supported by Miss Sybil Bennett and Mrs. Ellen Fairclough who gave tremendous help to that cause. Finally, in 1950, we got the government to establish a women's bureau. There have been some very distinguished women who have filled the position as directors of that bureau, and I think it was from then on that we began to get more interest in and concern for the welfare of the women of Canada.
In more recent years, when the report of the Royal Commission on the Status of Women was tabled it was this party that back in that year devoted one of its opposition days to the implementation of the recommendations in that report. I point out now that, in this session of the thirtieth parliament, we as the third party have only one opposition day that we can have with a vote, and we are giving that one day to this issue.
To go back two or three years, when the Anti-Inflation Board was established it was the leader of this party who directed one of his earliest criticisms at the failure of the regulations of that body to require arrangements to be made for a catch-up where the pay of women workers was deficient. Add to this the hundreds of times that some of us have argued for a better deal in terms of pensions for the women of this country and I think the record is a lot more clear than the government would like to recognize.
What I have said and what the speaker just before me has said underlines what I feel to be one of the areas in which discrimination against women is most severe. I feel that the time to correct discrimination is not in the next century, not 50 years from now, but right now. 1 am prepared to listen to speeches on the recommendations in the Florence Bird report which have been implemented, but I am more concerned about those that have not been touched; and I am particularly concerned about the unfairness and inequality that women suffer in their older years.
The hon. member for Kingston and the Islands pointed out that in terms of women by themselves, two-thirds of them between the ages of 65 and 70 are living at or below the poverty line and three-quarters of those over the age of 70 are living below the poverty line. That flows from certain definite causes. One is the fact that in the labour force they have fewer opportunities to get decent jobs with good pay, and so it follows that their pension income in later years is behind that of men.
It also follows from three or four situations that are built into our laws respecting pensions, and I want to spell out three or four of them and to insist that there should be no further delay in correcting these unfairnesses. First of all, the law and regulations regarding the spouse's allowance is about as cruel a law as there is on our statute books. The government makes out that there is something wonderfully equal about the spouse's allowance because it does not matter whether the spouse who gets that allowance is male or female; the younger husband can get it just as can the younger wife. But the statistics show that of the married couples in Canada between the ages of 60 and 65, in five out of six cases the husband is the older one; only in one case out of six is the husband the younger one. I suggest that in most of those cases where the husband is the younger member of the married couple he is able to keep working. So for all practical purposes, the spouse's allowance is a special provision for women.
Let us not get carried away with talk about the law in this respect being equal-it is a special provision for women. Look at what that legislation does to women. It does not give them a pension because they are women, because they are persons; it gives them a pension or allowance in relation to their attachment to a man. The woman does not stand on her own feet. She does not get something because she is entitled to it, because she needs it or has a right to it. She gets it only if she is attached to a man, only if she has a spouse 65 years of age or over. How can you justify a piece of legislation which, as I say, in practical terms is for women between the ages of 60 and 65 and then turn around and draw the line between those who have an older spouse and those who are single, divorced or separated?
The hon. member who preceded me and the wording of the amendment which has been proposed concentrate on a particular evil, namely the fact that if a woman in the age bracket of 60 to 65 loses her husband, she loses the spouse's allowance and she has nothing until the age of 65. That is so cruel that one wonders how it ever got enacted. We complained about this when it was brought in, but I say it is just as cruel to the woman who starts in her sixties as a widow or to the woman who is a spinster in her sixties. This whole piece of legislation is so fraught with unfairness and cruelty that in my view it should be taken back to the drawing boards and rewritten right away.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-EQUALITY OF RIGHTS FOR WOMEN IN LABOUR FORCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-EQUALITY OF RIGHTS FOR WOMEN IN LABOUR FORCE
speechtext:
The hon. member for York South (Mrs. Appolloni) made an impassioned plea this afternoon for women to be recognized as persons of equal status. I must say to her credit that when we had this legislation before the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs she did not like its provisions. But she also said this afternoon that we should not blame the government for these things but rather blame the attitude of society.
I do blame the government for a piece of legislation which discriminates against women in the way that the spouse's allowance does. As I say, the government tries to make out

March 6, 1978

that the regulation is equal because the situation is the same for a man as it is for a woman. That is a piece of nonsense. As a matter of fact, the government tries to carry this through by refusing to give us statistics on how many recipients of the spouse's allowance are male and how many are female. It even goes a step further. When a woman loses her husband, it could be the same as a man losing his wife, although I interject to say that I get letters on this every month and every letter I have had since this provision came into effect has been from a woman. I have never had a man between the ages of 60 and 65 write to me: "My old woman died and I lost my pension". No, it is women who suffer. The letter sent out from the department is one of those he/she letters: "Dear sir/madam, we are sorry that you lost your wife/husband", and so on down the line. It is completely heartless and the excuse for that is that the government does not like to keep statistics in terms of sex. This is the day of unisex. This is the day of equality. The result of this apparent attempt at equality is that women suffer in that respect, and suffer seriously.
I move on to the Canada Pension Plan, and here again I am completely in accord with the position taken by the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands, the position that I have been taking since the days back in 1964 and 1965 when we were putting that legislation through. No matter how much you try to say that the Canada Pension Plan is based on earnings from employment and therefore you cannot enrol housewives in it, Mr. Speaker, you are still denying the very thing that the Liberal member for York South wanted this afternoon, and that is the recognition of women as persons because of what they do, whether out in the work force or at home raising a family. If we are going to believe in that principle, if it is going to be asserted even, as I say, from the Liberal side of the House, it is time that we found a way to meet that situation.
I know all the arguments about the way it is set up in terms of a contribution based on income from employment, and maybe it has to be worked out in some other ways. When I make motions about this under Standing Order 43, I call for the equivalent of the Canada Pension Plan entitlement to be made available to women who are in the home. Certainly that should be done, or motions like this will have to be made year after year. The kind of speeches which were made this afternoon by the hon. Minister of State for Federal-Provincial Relations (Mr. Lalonde) and the hon. member for York South do not get away from this sort of situation. The Canada Pension Plan denial of any benefit to women who stay home and raise their families is a complete setting aside of all the fine words we heard this afternoon from the minister responsible for the status of women or from the hon. member for York South. I contend that is an area where improvements must be made right away.
I remind the House of my emphasis at the start, along with the statistics given earlier. We are concerned about the large majority of women who are at the poverty line in their retirement years. The reasons that happens are several, includ-
Status of Women
ing the kinds of things I have already talked about-the unfairness of the spouse's allowance and, particularly, the unfairness of the Canada Pension Plan in its denial of recognition that women in the home are contributing to our society just as much as women out in the work force.
This afternoon the hon. member for York South did not like the leader of my party placing so much emphasis on the right of women to have jobs. She wants women to be free to make their choice: to go out in the work force or stay at home. It is fine to have that choice, but if choosing to go out in the work force means a pension and some protection for old age, and staying at home means no adequate pension in old age, then certainly it is not a free choice at all. I contend the Canada Pension Plan needs to be improved in that respect without delay.
The minister responsible for the status of women this afternoon boasted about the amendments made to the Canada Pension Plan a year or so ago, under which at marriage breakdown the assets the two parties have accumulated can be split 50-50. In other words, they have to die or break up their marriages to receive the benefit. What about women having rights as women, rights as persons, rights as half the people of our population?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-EQUALITY OF RIGHTS FOR WOMEN IN LABOUR FORCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-EQUALITY OF RIGHTS FOR WOMEN IN LABOUR FORCE
speechtext:
There is another area where we have been grossly unfair to women. It runs through our society. It has been in existence for years and years. That does not make it right, just because society has accepted it. I am referring to the stupid arrangement under the public service superannuation plan, and most private pension plans, which works as follows. A man and a woman live together, build their home, assets and all the rest of it. They reach retirement and go on pension. He was not the only one to earn it. He and she earned it together. If she dies, his pension is 100 per cent; but if he dies first, her pension is 50 per cent. In any place where people believe in common sense, how can that arrangement be justified? It was a nice concession! We were doing something for the poor widows by giving them 50 per cent of their husbands' pensions! But it is not just, and it accounts for these ghastly statistics showing that two-thirds of our women between ages 65 and 70 and three-quarters of the women over 70 are in this situation. The place to correct that is in the public service superannuation plan. The reason it should be started there is to give the lead to private plans.
We have done a little better for the widows of members of parliament. Our pension plan is better in all respects than other pension plans. We provide 60 per cent for our widows. Why should it not be 75 or 80 per cent for all widows? Why should it not be 80 or 90 per cent for the wife if she survives, and 80 or 90 per cent for the man if he survives? The idea of 100 per cent for the man and 50 per cent for the woman, or even 100 per cent for the member of parliament and 60 per cent for the widow of a member of parliament, just does not stand up. It cannot be justified at all. As long as that kind of

March 6, 1978
Status of Women
arrangement exists in public service pensions, of course it will exist in the plans of the private world as well. The Canadian National Railways pension plan and the Canadian Pacific Railway pension plan operate in that manner as well. As a matter of fact, there are still pension plans which do not make all provisions for women and those which provide different conditions for women than for men.
A few nights ago that excellent documentary on the life of Nellie McClung was replayed. Those who watched it will remember the horror which was expressed by Nellie McClung when it was discovered that disability policies sold in those days provided a benefit in the case of death for a man or a woman, but there was no benefit for a woman in the case of disability, only for a man. The argument was that if women knew they could receive a benefit for disability, they might disfigure themselves or do something like that. In the documentary Mr. McClung was transferred to Alberta, because he was in the insurance business and his company could not stand the complaints his wife was making about that discriminatory provision.
That was in the dark ages which some of us remember, but it is still true that provisions exist in pension plans out in the private world which are unfair to women, and there are women who still do not receive the same benefits as men. It was not long ago that there were more inequalities in the public service system. Some of them have been ironed out, but the basic fact is still there: we provide better pensions for men than we do for women. When the death of one partner or the other occurs, it is the man who receives the gravy and it is the woman who receives only one-half of her rights.
With regard to the veterans' legislation, the same is true. That legislation is being improved. It is becoming pretty good compared with what it was a few years ago. But the widows of veterans still receive their pension rights only in terms of what the men's rights were. The woman who was a wife and looked after a veteran on a pension of 50 per cent or more upon his death receives the full widow's pension; but the wife who looked after a veteran on a pension of 45 or 47 per cent upon his death receives nothing. It is not what she may need, nor what she has done, which entitles her to a certain pension. It is what her attachment was to a man.
I would like to agree with the statements made by the hon. member for York South tonight concerning the desire that women be treated as persons and not because of their relationship to men, but I challenge her statement that the government is not to be blamed for this. These elements of discrimination are running through government legislation. We have been pressing for these improvements for a long time. As my leader pointed out this afternoon, we are concerned about the employment situation as well as the rights of native women. We have supported their moves and their organizations, as we have supported women in all of their efforts.
If your Honour will permit me another 30 seconds, I should like to indicate that discrimination is at its worst at the time of retirement where it ought not to be at all. We want these pension inequalities corrected. This can be brought about by

passing both the amendment and the motion now before the House.

speakeroldname: Mr. Raymond Dupont (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-EQUALITY OF RIGHTS FOR WOMEN IN LABOUR FORCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have only one reproach for the members of the opposition who have started in the House today a debate on the status of women and it is that they should have done so earlier. That is what the minister responsible for the status of women said on February 17 last in response to questions asked by the hon. member for Egmont (Mr. MacDonald) whom he was congratulating for his sudden interest in the status of women, reminding him that as the new Human Rights Commission was about to begin its operations two of the three commissioners were women.
Mr. Speaker, the fate of the Canadian woman attracts the envy of women the world over; this is news to nobody in the House. It is clear that the situation can and must be considerably improved, but if we look at what the situation is in other countries, we see that we have numerous reasons to be proud and to look forward to future improvements. As a matter of fact, in my capacity as Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration, I would like to point out today what has happened not only within the commission but for the benefit of the population as a whole through various manpower and unemployment insurance services. But I will preface my remarks with a brief outlook of the situation of women within the labour force. The minister in charge of the status of women has dwelt at quite some length on this matter, so I will limit myself to the main facts.
In 1966, 34 per cent of women participated in the paid labour force. In 1977, this rate of participation reached 46 per cent. Most of this increase originated in the 24 to 44 age group whose participation rate has gone up 59 per cent during the last decade. As mentioned before, unfortunately the rate of unemployment among women has also increased rapidly. In 1977, there were more women within the idle work force, at 45 per cent, than in the whole labour force, at 37 per cent. It has been suggested at times that female unemployment is not really alarming since their work contributes more to make up the family revenue and can serve at best to make some ready money or to allow for some luxuries. Statistics on the rate of employment and family income easily refute those allegations. Of the 4,022,000 women who worked in 1977, 30.1 per cent were single and 8.5 per cent were separated, widowed or divorced.
Mr. Speaker, the fact that those women have to work, strictly from an economic point of view, has never been doubted. Still, the work of women as second wage-earners in the family has at times been met with skepticism. That attitude does not take economic realities into account. In 1975, 70 per cent of all families in which women worked for pay had an income of less than $15,000 from the husband while the average family income was $16,113. In other words, the family
March 6, 1978

income would have been lower than the average income had the woman not worked. It is also sometimes said that women take over men's jobs. Mr. Speaker, the truth is entirely different. As the minister in charge of the status of women pointed out, women unfortunately still hold jobs that are generally considered as women's jobs, and are still generally nowhere to be seen in job areas traditionally reserved for men. We know, for instance, that if all the women in professional jobs were to leave the labour force tomorrow, without registering for unemployment insurance, the rate of unemployment would not go down by .5 per cent. Mr. Speaker, I hurry to add that the existence of ghettos in the field of employment seems most regrettable to us, and we spare no effort to remedy that situation. One must come to the conclusion that, in the future, men and women will increasingly perform the same type of work. We are nevertheless convinced that, to be prosperous, our economy will need all its resources.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to deal briefly with what the employment and immigration commission could do to improve the lot of women in the labour force. As far as favouring equal job opportunities is concerned, it should actively promote the expansion of the labour market which makes full use of womanpower potential and help workers seeking more rewarding and self-fulfilling jobs find them.
Mr. Speaker, this main objective can be divided into five sub-objectives: one, help women get the necessary knowledge and experience to join or rejoin the labour force; two, help women find jobs in line with their qualifications and abilities; three, help women make a more sophisticated choice in the whole spectrum of trades and professions which are in demand on the Canadian labour market; four, help employers identify and eliminate impediments to the hiring and promotion of women; five, encourage women to apply for work in industries for better paid jobs in the fields where they have traditionally been under-represented.
Mr. Speaker, my intention here is not to give a detailed account of the steps we are taking to fight discriminatory practices in the labour market, nor of the steps taken to counterbalance the effects of discriminatory practices which have affected women at the economic level. I would rather give some precise facts. In 1975-76, 33.9 per cent of successful applicants for the Canada manpower training program were women. However we must point out that the distribution of these women varied very much according to the type of training. They represented 53 per cent of trainees in the basic training for skill development, generally called upgrading course, 38.5 per cent in the vocational training program but only 2.8 per cent in the apprenticeship training program.
This problem is particularly difficult to solve since it is in the industry's new ventures that most openings will be found. The Foothills project, which has been referred to earlier today,
Status of Women
is a good example of our future ventures. It becomes essential that women receive a formation that will help them benefit from this evolution. To help women acquire these skills, the commission has greatly increased the number of courses given for their benefit. In one of these courses, women interested in trades traditionally reserved for men can gain practical experience in those trades. I want to mention two examples of this type of course: the basic trade courses for women given in Manitoba, and the introductory courses to so-called "non feminine" professions given in several centers in Ontario and Manitoba. There are also some vocational guidance courses directed to older women interested in joining the labour force for the first time or in returning to it.
Here is an example: the vocational guidance course for women given at Fredericton, New Brunswick. There is a similar program in Quebec, which is financed under the Canada manpower development program. Its goal is to develop and test various training instruments and programs that would help women better benefit from the training they have received under the Canada manpower development program, in view of their future return to the labour force.
Mr. Speaker, we ask our various manpower centers to establish a quota for female participation in the vocational guidance program, in a number of areas that are generally men's strongholds. We hope the provinces will do the same for their apprenticeship programs. Until the established quota is reached, women will be given priority for enrollment in these courses. A general information campaign will be set up accordingly.
As for the industrial manpower training program, we point out in our regional offices those trades where women are under-represented. We have asked each employment centre to designate one adviser charged with the promotion of industrial training programs among women. Objectives are chosen according to the number of women that have real chances of finding a job in those trades.
The community employment strategy is also used to encourage women to participate in training programs in various areas, including the contemporaneous program for woman heads of families in Regina, the native women's co-operative and also a program in Nova Scotia for women heads of families. The latter program has been in existence for some time. It includes workshops for women wishing to rejoin the work force, job training courses on housing renovation, employer-employee workshops on barriers to employment, and a co-operative training program in co-operation with the city of Halifax. While progress is made in our training programs, there remains an area where numerous efforts are still needed, namely apprenticeship as I mentioned earlier. Although apprenticeship is entirely under provincial jurisdiction, the federal government makes substantial financial contributions toward it. Mr. Speaker, we hope that the provinces will take the necessary steps to eliminate the discriminatory practices
3500

March 6, 1978
Status of Women
that are traditionally taking place against women in that kind of programs. We asked all our regional officers to appoint a senior officer responsible for co-ordinating the activities of the various regional apprenticeship programs to promote women's participation in those programs. Business leaders and unions must also change their practices in this area.
Let us now turn to counselling. Our employment offices have often been blamed for not providing an adequate service to women. The Employment and Immigration Commission is taking the necessary measures to correct the situation. A special training section on the problems of women will be included in the counsellors' vocational extension program. That section will be operational this spring. Mr. Speaker, I would like to draw your attention on several new and important facts that took place in recent months which will enable us to help women fully develop their potential in the labour market.
That program is Affirmative Action which can now be implemented at the federal level as well as in most provinces as a result of the passage of the Canadian Human Rights Act. The Affirmative Action concept which comes from the United States is now being considered in Canada as the only effective way of dealing with systems, attitudes and behaviour promoting inequities between men and women in the labour market. This approach or methodology is not restricted to women and could be used by other groups which could come under systematic discrimination. It is also intended to remove discrimination in hiring consisting in excluding certain groups or people when this is not warranted by any practical imperative, whether it be at the business level or the job to be filled. In other words, Affirmative Action deals with the roots rather than the symptoms of the problem.
Even if we do not know yet which body will finally be charged with carrying out federal activity in that regard, it is obvious that the commission will have a leading role to play and it is already getting prepared with tune-up operations. The Minister asked the commission to set up an Affirmative Action division to polarize the efforts of the commission in that respect.
It should also be pointed out that the status of working women is also being considered in the more important studies being made on unemployment. The studies examine among other things employment and unemployment statistics for women, their effort as the main breadwinner as well as the social and institutional barriers impeding their full participation in the labour market.
Mr. Speaker, I should now like to speak for a few moments about the efforts of the employment and immigration commission as an employer in terms of what is being done to improve opportunities for female employees.

The commission's equal opportunities for women program began in 1972 and progress was slow but steady in increasing female representation. Nevertheless, the commission was anxious to achieve even greater results and therefore in 1977, in order to speed up the process, it developed a five-year equal opportunities for women plan. This plan was based on the rationale that female representation in all categories, groups and levels should reflect women's representation in the national and provincial full-time labour forces. In fact, this rationale became the official policy of the organization concerning its work force. In other words, we are aiming for a work force which is in similar proportion to that of the labour force.
Using the rationale as described, goals were set for each of the major occupational groups in the commission. Our plan is ambitious but the minister and senior management of the commission are determined that concentrated effort can make it successful. Already, we see encouraging results. For example, there has been a gradual shift in the distribution of women throughout the organization. Last year at this time approximately 75 per cent of all female employees were in the administrative support category-the category which is often described as the ghetto category. This year we find that this distribution has dropped to 75 per cent, and we also find that women are at the higher levels of the category in increasing proportions.
Another example is the administrative and foreign service category, generally perceived as the middle management category. Last year women comprised only 26 per cent of its total. This has now risen to 28 per cent.
As well we find that, within the category itself, women have considerably improved their standing in every major group. To give but two examples, in the program administration group and the personnel administration group particularly women have been appointed for the first time at the highest levels.
There is also abundant evidence that women are improving their career mobility opportunities through mechanisms such as staff training programs. These vehicles are assisting substantial numbers of women in moving from the so-called ghetto category to the officer levels.
Concerning the senior executive category, the commission is aiming to have 10 per cent of that category represented by women by 1982. At this point there are only three women in the category but I am confident the goal will be reached.
The sample results which I have just described have not come about by accident. Rather, they are the culmination of efforts to build the concerns of women directly into the overall management system. I am proud to say that the commission is creating a personnel system, the mechanisms of which ensure that equal opportunities for women are taken into account in all its ensuing policies, practices and procedures. As well, I might mention that there are active programs in every region which support our objectives. Individual managers are responsible for the improved representation of women and are being held accountable for their results.
March 6, 1978

Without further elaboration I would only add that, as an employer, the department and commission have concrete plans to improve the position of women, that it is vigorously implementing those plans, and that it is experiencing very positive results. We believe that we can display methodology and results to both public and private sector employers as an example to be followed.
In conclusion, I would leave the House with two clear messages: first, the employment and immigration commission will continue its efforts to improve the situation of women in the labour force; second, it shall continue to create within the commission an environment in which women will be encouraged to realize their full potential.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-EQUALITY OF RIGHTS FOR WOMEN IN LABOUR FORCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would certainly want to identify at the outset with the remarks made by my colleague from Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald) as well as those of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) when they both mentioned it was the height of irony that we should need a special debate to deal with more than 50 per cent of the population of this country who still continue to suffer from some real discrimination in the area of economic matters.
I must admit when I listened this afternoon to the minister responsible for women, the Minister of State for Federal-Provincial Relations (Mr. Lalonde), that my first reaction was one of anger, then one of amazement and finally one of sadness. For any minister to present such a pathetic diatribe on such a vital issue is really a shocking case of irresponsibility. In view of the problems that many thousands of women are faced with today both in the private sector and in the public service respecting employment, that kind of a speech does them a disservice.
For the minister to try and extricate himself by making cheap political shots at members on this side of the House or anywhere is nothing short of amazing. I find his response both shallow and hollow to a great degree, more than I would have expected from him. I am sorry the minister is not here to hear me say this this evening. Quite frankly, I would have had more respect for this minister had he not made that kind of presentation today.
I make no apologies for taking part in this debate, Mr. Speaker, nor for the interest I have shown in recent weeks with respect to the problems which women are encountering, particularly in the public service. Members may know that it was some time last fall when I assumed responsibility as the opposition spokensman for the status of women, taking over that assignment from my colleague for the former hon. member for Fundy-Royal, Mr. Gordon Fairweather. He now chairs, in a very distinguished way, the new Human Rights Commission. I hope I follow him in the line of his particular interest and commitment in terms of trying to deal responsibly and rationally with a major problem that confronts us in society today.
Status of Women
When the minister begins to use statistics, as he did this afternoon, and talks about a 50 per cent improvement with respect to government appointments through orders in council, I find this is about the most meaningless kind of endeavour he could engage in. He is not even being consistent with himself. Earlier through a quarterly newsletter he claimed that figures show 115 per cent more women appointed in 1976. Perhaps he is becoming more cautious in the use of these meaningless statistics. As we all know, statistics can say anything you want them to.
Nothing has been more the focus of attention in recent weeks that appointments to senior levels of the public service, the SX category. In a letter that I received dated October 17, 1977 from the research and analysis officer of the Public Service Commission, these statistics were stated. As I say, statistics can be used any way you want. In 1973 in the senior executive category of the Public Service Commission we had 859 men and nine women. In 1974 there were 1,053 men and 18 women. In 1975 there were 1,165 men and 21 women; and in 1976, 1,238 men and 30 women. You could, of course, mention that between 1973 and 1974, the year the minister took office, there was a 100 per cent increase in women in the SX category; the figure went from nine to 18. The fact that the number only increased from 18 to 21 women from 1974 to 1975 means the percentage increase was 16% per cent. In 1976 the increase from 21 to 30 women meant there was a 45 per cent increase over 1975. In other words, in that time period in 1974 there was an increase of 194 men in the SX category and nine women, in 1975, 112 men and 12 women, and in 1976, 173 men and women. One thing is abundantly clear from those statistics: there is no great plan of action on the part of this government to remove discrimination at senior levels of the public service.
When the minister wants to score Brownie points by attacking members on this side for discovering a latent interest in the status of women, I suppose we have to accept that. That is the nature of political warfare. But what I am more concerned with is the situation that forces a number of female public servants to issue the kind of anonymous report which ironically enough I released the same day the minister was exposing his great "plan of action" for documenting, through the use of the statistics of the Public Service Commission itself, not only the present discrimination that exists with respect to public service employment but the increasing discrimination that is taking place at middle and upper level of management.
There is no way in the world that the minister responsible for the status of women, or any other minister in this House, can explain those statistics away unless they are prepared to be a good deal more forthright than they have been to date. I mentioned that the minister has now released his latest plan of action which is to take us to 1985 with respect to equal opportunities. But the minister has in no way indicated what all these various experts and task forces are actually going to do by way of any clear cut goals, strategy or any methods of implementation. Even more, he has not had the courtesy to issue the kind of report that he himself said would be necessary
80033-9%

March 6, 1978
Status of Women
some years ago. The report of the advisory council on the status of women dated June, 1977, in documenting the situation of women in the public service, concludes:
Publication of the Advisory Council's first study on Women in the Public Service in the fall of 1975 prompted the Minister responsible for the Status of Women to say publicly "it is quite apparent that a more explicit and aggressive policy is required which will involve the active commitment of departments to accelerate the desegregation of the Public Service work force." The special measures announced by the Minister in October 1975 included an annual review of the progress achieved by each department.
Where are those annual reviews? Where is the public accounting that was to take place that the minister publicly endorsed and said would take place in succeedings years in 1976 and 1977? What we have is the minister hoping, by some kind of subterfuge, by some new announcement of more experts and more task forces, to indicate that at some time, perhaps in 1985, we will have a clear accounting as to the actual situation of women in the public service. There are thousands and thousands of women in the public service who will not wait that long. As proven by this report, they are already acknowledging that there are signs of increasing discrimination against women workers.
It is a fallacy that women are the cause of the high unemployment rate today. My colleague, the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands, I think very effectively and eloquently in her speech exposed the kind of damaging myth that is fostered when that kind of attribution is made. Certainly the Minister for Employment and Immigration (Mr. Cullen), the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) and even the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) have furthered the mythology that in some way or other women are the cause of the present unemployment difficulties that this country is faced with and with which the government is failing to deal adequately.
In a recent publication from Statistics Canada it was clearly shown that, contrary to what the minister responsible for the status of women has said, the entrance rate into the work force has declined in recent years simply because women are faced, as everyone is, with increasing difficulty in finding any kind of meaningful employment. Where are women finding employment? They are finding it at less than adequate wages and they do the kinds of servile tasks that for the most part men are simply not willing to do.
My colleague from Kingston and the Islands has also mentioned the particularly acute problem faced by women over the age of 60 and the failure of this government to deal adequately with that problem. I suppose if there is any one tragic aspect to the minister's speech this afternoon, from my point of view as well as that of all members of this House it was that the minister missed a golden opportunity. It is generally acknowledged, except by the most blind, that there are particular problems today in the work force both in the private sector and in the public sector with respect to the employment of women. It would have been a service in his capacity as minister responsible to have identified those pressures, those myths referred to by my colleague, the problems making it more difficult at the present time to implement equal opportunity programs. Instead, what did the minister do? He ran through

a shopping list that, as the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) said, was so barren that he had to repeat it in both official languages.
The minister did not even take the opportunity to identify some of the key pressure points and problems today for women in the work force. He at no time tried to identify what the specific goals must be of a society really trying to achieve some kind of economic justice. There was no clear accounting as to his role since 1974 when he was appointed to this important post, and no indication of the particular problems we are faced with today. I do not know whether the government still does not know or whether it just does not care, but certainly it is very clear it is not acting. In not acting, it is contributing to the situation, certainly to a very great misunderstanding.
I sent a copy of the report that I released on February 16 to the minister. That is about two and a half weeks ago. To my knowledge, he has in no way attempted to respond to that report. The only response that I have seen in fact came from no minister at all but from somebody speaking for the chairman of the Public Service Commission, Johanna Hickey, director of the Office of Equal Opportunity. She said that this report was full of distortion, blatant error and emotionalism. I wonder when we will get the facts to document those kinds of charges, either from Ms. Hickey or anyone else who speaks for the Public Service Commission.
Within a few days of that comment, on February 22, these public servants, again through me, issued a further comment in response to that criticism. I quote one part of it:
Well, as we said, we have nothing to hide so here are the facts: as of December 1976, there were 2,927 persons in the Personnel Administration (PE) group in the federal public service of Canada. Of these, 778 were women (nearly 27 per cent). The PE group has seven levels, with PE 1 being the lowest level. In most departments, the Director of Personnel would be a PE 7 or an SX, but in some smaller organizations, he or she (we couldn't find a "she"!) might be a PE 6. The breakdown for the PE group is as follows. Again the information is from the Public Service Staff Relations Board Pay Research Bureau Report.
What we Find is that in levels one through four the participation is very heavily loaded toward women; but as it increases through levels five, six and seven we notice a rapidly dropping percentage of women and a rapidly increasing one for men. That is within the public service itself. I am waiting anxiously to find out what kind of report we are going to get on that statistic from the minister or from somebody who will speak on behalf of the Public Service Commission.
Just today I received some further information with regard to the post office. I am sorry the Postmaster General (Mr. Lamontagne) is not here this evening; he was here for a while this afternoon. The post office seems to be one of the most blatant areas in terms of discrimination against women in the work force.
In the earlier report that was released, in the listing of senior employees at the SX level it will be noticed that the post office is the largest employing department in the federal government, employing some 55,000 people, 20 per cent of whom are
March 6, 1978

women. There are 43 people at the SX category, but to my knowledge there is still not one woman.
I want to read a few observations that have been made with regard to the situation in the post office at the present time. For women at the PE or 04 level and above, for 1973 and 1977 there is almost no change. In fact, in that four year period the increase has been something like .91 per cent. That means that perhaps the number has gone from something like three women in 1973 to something like nine in 1977.
In most samples of this size-that is, a group of over 500- this would be called negligible. In fact, an increase of 1 per cent is really not worth anything. That is the situation that prevails in the post office, an area where there has been literally no act of representation or equal opportunity program at work. The other interesting comment as a result of this later document came from the Minister of Employment and Immigration, who I am sorry is not here tonight. He took the opportunity of issuing a press release, again with a number of self-serving and partial percentages, on March 2 and took serious issue with some of the things said in the two earlier reports and releases.
I will not take the time of the House this evening to review the kind of misleading data that the Minister of Employment and Immigration put on the record. The information in the press release does in his own case. On the second page of his press release, which deals with the administrative support category representation, he talks about the CR 5. It is interesting to note-and this is obviously not a major management and decision making area-that whereas in 1976 there were 30.1 per cent males and 69.9 per cent females, in 1977 the figure for males had dropped to 28.6 per cent and the figure for females had increased to 71.4 per cent. That is an obvious female ghetto if ever there was one!
This is the kind of misleading information that the government to this date is putting on the record with regard to its stewardship in terms of equal opportunity programs for women in the public service. What we obviously need, and what I thought we would get when I saw the motion put down last week by the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby (Mr. Broad-bent), is a frank accounting of the government's responsibility in this area for at least the period that this government, and particularly this minister, have been responsible for the status of women, which is about three and a half years. But what did we get? We got a pathetic political diatribe and nothing else.
No other minister has taken part in this debate. We had a speech from one parliamentary secretary. Perhaps we will have another. We have certainly had nothing substantial from the members of the government who carry responsibility in this area.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-EQUALITY OF RIGHTS FOR WOMEN IN LABOUR FORCE
speechtext: There is not a minister in the House.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-EQUALITY OF RIGHTS FOR WOMEN IN LABOUR FORCE
speechtext:
That further amplifies their disinterest or disdain for this topic. Surely the government must now state publicly what its goals are. It is not enough for a minister to have a meeting outside the House in the Pearson building with those who are his fans or friends in terms of the
Status of Women
status of women and not come before this House as the minister responsible to make a clear-cut statement as to his goals objectives.
Why did he not have the courage and common sense to say what the strategy of the government will be with regard to the serious problems confronting women? What has he to tell us about the kinds of costs and benefits that will result from substantial change within the public service? The government is simply failing in its leadership in this area. In fact, the leadership is simply non-existent.
In 1975 we had International Women's Year. We have had literally nothing similar since then. In fact, as these women public servants have acknowledged, we see a deteriorating situation with regard to attitudes and programs within the public service.
In addition to the motion of the New Democratic Party, we have put down some suggestions by way of amendment which now seem to be generally accepted, at least on this side of the House. These are some specifics that we had hoped the minister or others would have talked on. Certainly the advisory council on the status of women has filled hundreds of pages with clear-cut recommendations. The minister said they would like to take action on the amendment to the Indian Act. How often do we have to hear him make that kind of statement before anything substantial happens? I happen to have a private member's bill on that subject. If the minister really wanted to do something, it could be moved forward to the standing committee.
With regard to the tax changes that have been suggested, surely a clear inequity is the problem of women who work with their husbands on farms, in rural situations, in fishing operations or in small businesses. They are not provided with the same benefits they would have in a legal partnership or an incorporated set up. The advisory council on the status of women made ample recommendations in this regard.
My colleague, the hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Hargrave), recently received a letter from one of his constituents. With his permission and yours, Mr. Speaker, I will quote a couple of phrases from it. This woman writes:
I work on the farm full time (this often means 12 or more hours per day) during calving, seeding, summer fallowing and harvesting as well as doing all the bookkeeping and helping whenever necessary during other times. You will find that this is also the case with most of the women in this area, as it is no doubt in every farming community throughout Canada ...
My husband has threatened to divorce me, and then hire me as a farm worker and so claim wages for me as an expense for income tax purposes. I am only joking, but I do think that the fact that this could be a solution, points out the foolishness of the present tax law. Just as silly is the fact that I could do the same work I do on our farm for a neighbour and get paid for it and my husband could hire a neighbour's wife to do the work I am doing here, pay her and deduct her wages as an expense.
It also hurts to know that women who work at their own job can file their own income tax. I have a teacher's certificate, but when I got married I decided to give up teaching to raise a family and help out on the farm. I feel this has been a good decision as far as the family is concerned and has meant a rewarding way of life to me but the present tax laws do not encourage anyone to make such a choice.

March 6, 1978
Status of Women
In the face of that reasonable proposition, could not the minister urge his colleague the Minister of Finance to include a provision of the kind suggested in a budgetary announcement? If this debate today does nothing else, I hope it will wake up the minister and the government who seem to be immobilized at the present time in the face of a pressing national issue.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-EQUALITY OF RIGHTS FOR WOMEN IN LABOUR FORCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in the light of the comments just made by the hon. member for Egmont (Mr. MacDonald) I think I should say at the outset of my remarks that several ministers have been unable to be here today. The Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Cullen) is unable to be here. The Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford) is ill and I am speaking in his place. I would also point out that there are two ministers sitting here now and that they were sitting here at the time the hon. member made his complaint that there were no ministers in the House.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-EQUALITY OF RIGHTS FOR WOMEN IN LABOUR FORCE
speechtext: We want real ministers!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-EQUALITY OF RIGHTS FOR WOMEN IN LABOUR FORCE
speechtext: All of us on this side of the House were pleasantly surprised that the NDP were presenting us with an opportunity to speak about our record in the field of women's rights, because that record is one of which the government has a right to be proud.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-EQUALITY OF RIGHTS FOR WOMEN IN LABOUR FORCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-EQUALITY OF RIGHTS FOR WOMEN IN LABOUR FORCE
speechtext: I would not want to be misunderstood, Mr. Speaker. There are many things which need to be done in this area, especially on the side of implementation. The opposition has rightly been drawing attention to these things. There will always be weaknesses to remedy, Mr. Speaker, because here we are faced with a great historic inequity, probably the greatest inequity existing in the world today. An inequity of this dimension is not something which can be cleared up overnight. Nevertheless, Canada is on the leading edge of the movement to advance women's rights throughout the world and this government certainly has by far the best record of any government in Canada in this field.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-EQUALITY OF RIGHTS FOR WOMEN IN LABOUR FORCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-EQUALITY OF RIGHTS FOR WOMEN IN LABOUR FORCE
speechtext:
I am sure the NDP faced something of a dilemma when making women's rights the subject of today's debate. They wanted to get in on a good thing but obviously did not wish to give the government the credit which its record deserves. I thought the solution of the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby (Mr. Broadbent) was rather ingenuous. He got around this difficulty by avoiding the subject entirely, by dealing with peripheral aspects of the problem, by making comments which from his limited viewpoint he could have made about any minority group in the country-youth, Cape Breton miners, the urban poor or what have you. He really did not deal with the question of women's rights at all.
In the words of the motion before us today, the NDP asserts that the women of Canada ought to have fully equal rights in

participating in the Canadian economy. Mr. Speaker, where was that party last spring when the government brought forward the Canadian Human Rights Act? If the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Leggatt) had been able to be here today I know he would have brought to the attention of his colleagues section two of that legislation which was passed by the House. It reads as follows:
Every individual should have an equal opportunity with other individuals to make for himself or herself the life that he or she is able or wishes to have consistent with his or her duties and obligations as a member of society without being hindered in or prevented from doing so by discriminatory practices.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-EQUALITY OF RIGHTS FOR WOMEN IN LABOUR FORCE
speechtext: Fine words!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-EQUALITY OF RIGHTS FOR WOMEN IN LABOUR FORCE
speechtext:
They are indeed fine words and a former member of this House has been given the authority to enforce those words.
Three elements of the Human Rights Act are of particular interest to women. First, sex is made a prohibited ground of discrimination in employment and in the provision of services. Second, provision is made for affirmative action programs and the Human Rights Commission is enabled to advise on and encourage the setting up of these special programs. Third, and most significant, the legislation establishes the principle of equal pay for work of equal value. This is the first government and the only government in the country to take this step. Enactment of this principle is one of the most significant advances in recent years in the march for equality for women and puts Canada ahead of almost every jurisdiction in the world.
The wording "equal pay for work of equal value" is significant and is more effective in its formulation than that used in other jurisdictions whose legislation may appear to be similar but is not because it uses the concept of equal pay for similar work. When the government was drafting the Human Rights Act it listened to women's organizations who explained how under the similar work formulation women employees could be laid off into the low pay job ghettos where they would never have a chance to do work similar to that of men, job ghettos where women could be paid less even though their work was of equal value. The government accepted this principle of equal value and put it into the legislation.
The over-all significance of the affirmative action power of the commission can hardly be overestimated. In addition to the right to make recommendations as to special programs, the commission also has the power, where discrimination has been established against an employer by a hearing tribunal, to order an affirmative action program to be instituted at the expense of the employer. In this area the American experience has suggested that affirmative action programs are a much more useful device to disadvantaged minorities than are a host of individual complaints which, even collectively, cannot usually bring about a change in the practice of an employer.
I would point out, Mr. Speaker, that the record of the NDP in this area has been dismal. They have had many opportunities over the last five years to respond to the needs of women. In British Columbia under the former premier, Mr. Barrett, in
March 6, 1978

Manitoba under the former premier, Mr. Schreyer, and still in Saskatchewan for a short time, under the premiership of Mr. Blakeney, they could have enacted legislation to give effect to the concept of equal pay for work of equal value.
Did that party which today preaches in its motion that the women of Canada ought to have fully equal rights participating in the Canadian economy ever lift a finger when it had the power to do so in those provinces? Did it ever put in place such legislation? Not once. A sad comment on a party which used to think of itself as a leading force of social reform in Canada.
Perhaps I should also draw attention to the new committee which the Conservative party has established in this election year-a caucus committee on the status of women. I believe the first public pronouncement of that body was that no serious consideration had been given to women's issues in parliament for the past two years. Well, where was the Conservative party last summer when we enacted the Human Rights Act? The hon. member for Egmont mentioned the former member for Fundy-Royal who played a very vital part in that. He is playing an even more important part in it now that it has been enacted.
Where was the Conservative party when the Criminal Code was reformed to prevent the unnecessary harassment of rape victims appearing as witnesses? Where was it when we brought about the reforms outlined earlier in this debate by my colleagues?
The assertion that we have given no serious consideration to women's issues has a hollow ring to it in the face of all this. Hon. members in the official opposition would have served Canadian women better had they directed their criticisms at their colleagues in the government of Ontario, who have so far flatly refused to adopt the principle of equal pay for work of equal value.
One of the amendments proposed by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) suggested the government should take some action in relation to the tax situation of spouses working in unincorporated small businesses. This is an issue the government has been looking into. Unfortunately, it is not one which lends itself to a simple solution since it would be very difficult to monitor the payment of wages to a spouse. Nevertheless, a step in this direction has, in fact, been taken by Revenue Canada. A recent Revenue Canada interpretation bulletin goes some way toward equality of the sexes under income tax rules. It makes it easier for a husband and wife to establish a partnership to carry on a business and for the wife to receive income from the business which is treated for income tax purposes as her own. Without going into the detailed provisions of the policy statement, let me simply say that among other things it provides that, if a loan is made from husband to wife on terms which are comparable to those which one businessman might offer another operating at arm's length, such loan will be treated as a contribution of capital by the wife. In other words, this major policy change will allow a husband to finance his wife's capital contribution, albeit on a commercial basis, and for the wife to be considered a fully fledged partner for income tax purposes.
Status of Women
This recent bulletin is an indication that efforts are continuing to be made by the government to recognize the new realities relating to women in the work force. It suggests a new approach to tax treatment of husbands and wives while attempting to prevent tax fraud through artificial arrangements.
In conclusion, I want to draw attention to the fact that the individual and social cost of unfair discrimination on the basis of sex in our society is staggering. A person's ability to contribute to society is not determined by whether that person is a man or a woman; nor is his or her value to his or her employer so measured.

speechtext: Now you're telling it the way it is.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-EQUALITY OF RIGHTS FOR WOMEN IN LABOUR FORCE
speechtext: I have been doing it all along.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-EQUALITY OF RIGHTS FOR WOMEN IN LABOUR FORCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-EQUALITY OF RIGHTS FOR WOMEN IN LABOUR FORCE
speechtext: You sound like Bryce Mackasey. Take over Bryce's job.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-EQUALITY OF RIGHTS FOR WOMEN IN LABOUR FORCE
speechtext:
I should say to members of the opposition that I find my present job most satisfying. It will be a long time before they are going to get jobs on this side of the House.
As I mentioned, we are dealing with a great and historic social inequality. In fact, this is not really a problem of women's rights at all; it is a problem of common human rights because the various forms of sexual inequality involve our common humanity and are harmful to all people. It cannot be tolerated by society, and government and society must work together over the years to eliminate these problems.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-EQUALITY OF RIGHTS FOR WOMEN IN LABOUR FORCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the motion before the House gives sad evidence of the unemployment and underemployment of women in Canada today. In spite of the existence of the advisory council on the status of women, International Women's Year, and the minister in cabinet assigned to develop a national plan of action to respond to the needs of women in Canada, we have not, to paraphrase a popular ad, "come a long way, baby".
A few women have broken through the man-made barriers to participate fully in Canadian life. I am one of the lucky ones and I have found myself walking in new areas which have traditionally been men's preserves. I have found myself involved in making decisions that will affect the lifestyle of generations to come. I have felt pride and satisfaction, as it is right for women to be involved in decisions affecting society.
As the waves of rapid change have lately increased in their intensity, I am glad we are having a debate about the role of women so we can gain a sense of perspective about the world today, its challenges and how they affect women, why it is different for women today than at any other time in history, and what tasks must now be tackled by women together with men, faced with the fact that the population of the world will double in the space of a lifetime. By the time my 15 year old

March 6, 1978
Status of Women
daughter is my age, the population of this planet will have doubled to seven billion.
The capital, technology and management skills required to meet present needs were accumulated over thousands of years, but now we must more than double our productive capacity in the world as a whole, not simply in the rich countries but throughout the world, in a space of one lifetime. Planners looking at the resources needed to meet this incredible challenge are realizing that the most valuable untapped creative and management resource they have is womanpower.
